1.0.1.g: Vitruvius tells Imperator Caesar he held back his writings on architecture while Caesar was busy winning command of the world.

1.0.2.g: Seeing Caesar's care for public buildings, Vitruvius offers his work; he served Caesar's father and maintained ballistae and scorpiones, rewarded through Caesar's sister.

1.0.3.g: Freed from want by Caesar's favour, Vitruvius writes definite rules so Caesar can judge existing and future buildings; the books disclose all principles.

1.1.1.g: The architect needs many branches of learning; his knowledge is born of practice (manual work to a drawing) and theory (explaining by proportion).

1.1.2.g: Architects with manual skill but no scholarship gain no authority; pure theorists chase the shadow; those with both reach their object sooner.

1.1.3.g: Architecture has the thing signified and what gives it significance; the architect needs talent plus instruction in drawing, geometry, history, philosophy, music, medicine, law, astronomy.

1.1.4.g: Reasons for the studies: letters for lasting treatises, drawing for sketches, geometry for rule, compasses, square, level and plummet, optics for light, arithmetic for cost.

1.1.5.g: History explains ornament: Caryatides are statues of the enslaved matrons of Caryae, which sided with Persia, set to carry loads as lasting punishment.

1.1.6.g: After Plataea the Lacedaemonians under Pausanias built the Persian Porch from spoils, with statues of Persian captives in barbarian dress holding up the roof.

1.1.7.g: Philosophy makes the architect honest and free of avarice, and teaches physics, needed to prevent damage from air currents in water conduits.

1.1.8.g: Music lets the architect tune ballistae, catapultae and scorpiones: the twisted sinew strings on both sides must give the same note so the arms strike together.

1.1.9.g: Bronze sounding vessels (echeia) in niches under theatre seats are tuned to the fourth, fifth, octave up to double octave to strengthen the actor's voice.

1.1.10.g: Medicine is needed for climates, air, healthy sites and waters; law for party walls, eaves drip, drains, windows and contracts; astronomy for cardinal points and sundials.

1.1.11.g: Because the study is so vast, nobody may hastily call himself an architect without climbing from boyhood through these arts and sciences.

1.1.12.g: All studies share a common bond, so a liberal education is one body; Pytheos of Priene claimed the architect should surpass every specialist, which is not realized.

1.1.13.g: The architect cannot equal Aristarchus in philology, Aristoxenus in music, Apelles in painting, Myron or Polyclitus in sculpture, Hippocrates in medicine, yet must not be unskilled.

1.1.14.g: Even specialists in a single art rarely reach fame, so an architect skilled in many arts cannot be expected to surpass them all.

1.1.15.g: Pytheos erred: each art has work and theory; theory is common to scholars, as pulse rhythm to physician and musician, but the work belongs to the specialist.

1.1.16.g: Sciences share theory (astronomers with musicians and geometricians); a fair knowledge suffices the architect; rare men like Archytas, Eratosthenes and Archimedes become pure mathematicians.

1.1.17.g: Vitruvius asks Caesar and readers to pardon faults of grammar: he writes as an architect, not philosopher or rhetorician, yet promises real value to builders and scholars.

1.2.1.g: Architecture depends on six things: Order (taxis), Arrangement (diathesis), Eurythmy, Symmetry, Propriety and Economy (oikonomia).

1.2.2.g: Order is adjustment by quantity using modules taken from the work; Arrangement is proper placing, expressed in groundplan, elevation and perspective, born of reflexion and invention.

1.2.3.g: Eurythmy is beauty and fitness of the members: height suited to breadth, breadth to length, all corresponding symmetrically.

1.2.4.g: Symmetry is agreement of members with the whole from a standard part: column thickness or triglyph in temples, the hole in ballistae, tholepin space in ships.

1.2.5.g: Propriety by prescription: hypaethral temples for Jupiter Lightning, Heaven, Sun, Moon; Doric for Minerva, Mars, Hercules; Corinthian for Venus, Flora, Nymphs; Ionic for Juno, Diana, Bacchus.

1.2.6.g: Propriety by usage: magnificent interiors need elegant entrance-courts; dentils in a Doric cornice or triglyphs over Ionic cushion capitals spoil the effect.

1.2.7.g: Propriety by nature: healthy sites with springs for fanes of Aesculapius and Health; east light for bedrooms and libraries, west for winter baths, north for picture galleries.

1.2.8.g: Economy is thrifty management of materials and site: do not demand scarce pitsand, fir or marble; substitute river or sea sand, cypress, poplar, elm or pine.

1.2.9.g: Second stage of Economy: plan dwellings to suit each class, different for ordinary householders, town, country produce, money-lenders, the opulent, and statesmen.

1.3.1.g: Architecture has three departments: building, timepieces, machinery. Building is public or private; public buildings are defensive, religious or utilitarian (harbours, markets, colonnades, baths, theatres).

1.3.2.g: All must have durability (foundations to solid ground, good materials), convenience (faultless arrangement, right exposure) and beauty (pleasing appearance, members in symmetry).

1.4.1.g: A fortified town needs a healthy site: high, temperate, free of mist, frost and marshes; coastal sites facing south or west are unhealthy from heat.

1.4.2.g: Swings of heat and cooling harm inhabitants and things alike: wine rooms take light from the north, and granaries must be kept from the sun's course.

1.4.3.g: Heat dissolves things' strength and softens them, as iron heated in a furnace is easily worked and hardens again when dipped in cold water.

1.4.4.g: Summer heat weakens everyone and winter makes unhealthy districts healthier; people moved from cold to hot lands waste away, those moved north gain.

1.4.5.g: Towns must avoid districts of hot winds, for all bodies are compounded of four elements, heat, moisture, the earthy and air, mixed by temperament.

1.4.6.g: Excess of one element destroys the mixture: heat from the sky, moisture from damp winds, the earthy from overmuch food, air from heavy atmosphere.

1.4.7.g: Birds have much air and little earth and moisture, fish little moisture, land animals much moisture; hence each lives only in its own element.

1.4.8.g: Since animal bodies break up from excess or lack of an element, a very temperate climate must be chosen for the city, health being first requisite.

1.4.9.g: The ancestors sacrificed cattle that grazed on a proposed site and inspected their livers; repeatedly abnormal livers meant unhealthy food and water, so they moved elsewhere.

1.4.10.g: In Crete by the river Pothereus, cattle near Gnosus have normal spleens while those near Gortyna have almost none, from an herb the Cretans call asplenon.

1.4.11.g: A town in seaside marshes facing north or north-east and above shore level is healthy: ditches drain it and salt sea kills marsh creatures, as at Altino, Ravenna, Aquileia.

1.4.12.g: Stagnant marshes like the Pomptine putrefy; sickly Old Salpia in Apulia was moved by Marcus Hostilius four miles to a healthy seaside site with a lake harbour.

1.5.1.g: After securing health, food supply and transport, dig foundations for towers and walls down to solid bottom, much thicker than the wall above ground.

1.5.2.g: Towers project beyond the wall to flank attackers; roads approach gates from right to left exposing the unshielded side; towns should be circular, not square or with salient angles.

1.5.3.g: The wall should be thick enough for armed men to pass on top, and tied through with closely set charred olive wood ties, which never decay.

1.5.4.g: Towers stand no more than a bowshot apart; behind each tower the wall is interrupted for the tower's width and bridged by removable wooden flooring.

1.5.5.g: Towers must be round or polygonal, since battering rams shatter the angles of square ones; earthen ramparts make walls safest against rams and mining.

1.5.6.g: Ramparts are needed only where high ground outside allows a level assault; dig wide deep ditches and sink in them thick foundations to carry the earthwork.

1.5.7.g: Lay a second inner foundation leaving room for cohorts on the rampart top, and join the two with cross walls like saw teeth to divide the earth's thrust.

1.5.8.g: No fixed wall material can be prescribed: use dimension stone, flint, rubble, burnt or unburnt brick as found; Babylon used burnt brick with asphalt.

1.6.1.g: Lay out house lots, streets and alleys to exclude winds; Mytilene is badly placed: south wind brings illness, northwest coughs, north severe cold.

1.6.2.g: Wind is a flowing wave of air produced when heat meets moisture, shown by bronze eolipiles: hollow balls with water that blow a blast when heated.

1.6.3.g: Shutting out winds keeps the well healthy and helps cure catarrh, coughs, pleurisy and consumption, which agitated air worsens and mild thick air restores.

1.6.4.g: Some count four winds (Solanus, Auster, Favonius, Septentrio), but there are eight; Andronicus of Cyrrhus built Athens' octagonal marble tower with wind reliefs and a bronze Triton vane.

1.6.5.g: Eurus lies southeast between Solanus and Auster, Africus southwest, Caurus or Corus northwest, Aquilo northeast; the method of finding wind quarters follows.

1.6.6.g: Level a marble amussium in the city centre, set a bronze gnomon, mark the shadow tip at about the fifth hour, draw a circle, mark the equal afternoon shadow.

1.6.7.g: Intersecting arcs from the two points give the north-south line; a sixteenth of the circumference each side marks Auster and Septentrio; the rest divides into eight winds for street lines.

1.6.8.g: Streets facing the winds funnel blasts through narrow alleys; house lines must turn away so winds strike the angles of blocks and disperse.

1.6.9.g: Eratosthenes measured the earth's circumference as 252,000 stadia, or 31,500,000 paces; an eighth, 3,937,500 paces per wind, is wide enough for shifting breezes.

1.6.10.g: Lesser winds flank the eight: Leuconotus and Altanus by Auster, Libonotus and Subvesperus by Africus, Argestes and Etesiae by Favonius, and others to Eurocircias and Volturnus.

1.6.11.g: Morning breezes arise as the rising sun drives humid air, whence the names Eurus and aurion; doubts about Eratosthenes do not affect the wind quarters.

1.6.12.g: Two figures are given; with centre A and morning shadow point B draw a circle, mark afternoon point C, intersect arcs at D, line E F gives south-north.

1.6.13.g: Set off a sixteenth of the circumference each side of E and F (points G, H, I, K), divide the rest in threes (L, M, N, O) for eight wind spaces.

1.7.1.g: Forum by the harbour in a seaside city, else central; Jupiter, Juno, Minerva on the highest point; Mercury in the forum; Venus, Vulcan, Mars outside the walls.

1.7.2.g: Ceres belongs outside the city in a place visited only for sacrifice; temples and symmetry come in books three and four, materials in book two.

2.0.1.g: Dinocrates, tired of waiting for an introduction to Alexander, oils himself, dons lion skin, poplar chaplet and club, and walks to the king's tribunal.

2.0.2.g: Dinocrates tells Alexander his design: Mount Athos carved as a man holding a fortified city in his left hand, a water bowl in his right.

2.0.3.g: Alexander praises the Athos design but rejects the site: no cornfields nearby, and a city cannot thrive without food, as a baby without milk.

2.0.4.g: Dinocrates follows Alexander to Egypt and builds Alexandria by its natural harbour and Nile cornfields; Vitruvius, lacking looks, relies on knowledge and writings.

2.0.5.g: Book 1 covered architecture's scope and town sites; before temple proportions, this book treats building materials, prefixed by the origins of building.

2.1.1.g: Early men lived like beasts; storm-rubbed trees caught fire, people gathered at its warmth, and from signs and sounds speech arose.

2.1.2.g: Fire brought men into assembly; upright and dexterous, they built first shelters of green boughs, dug caves, or mud-and-twig refuges copied from swallows' nests.

2.1.3.g: By emulation huts improved: forked stakes with twigs daubed in mud, dried-mud walls roofed with reeds, then peaked sloping projecting roofs to shed rain.

2.1.4.g: Proof from foreign tribes: oak-shingle and thatch roofs in Gaul and Spain; Colchians stack crossed tree trunks into log towers with pyramidal tortoise roofs.

2.1.5.g: Timberless Phrygians trench a hillock and roof it with log pyramid, reeds and earth mounds; mud roofs survive at Marseilles, Areopagus, hut of Romulus.

2.1.6.g: From such relics ancient methods are inferred; practice made the skilled into carpenters, and reason led men from building to other arts and civilization.

2.1.7.g: Men gave up huts for houses with foundations, brick or stone walls, timber and tile roofs, reached rules of symmetry; materials will now be treated.

2.1.8.g: Vitruvius defends the book's position: Book 1 defined the art and the architect; this one treats materials and the origin and progress of building.

2.1.9.g: The book is in its proper place; materials will be explained by their elementary constituents, since everything consists of elementary particles and primary causes.

2.2.1.g: Primordial substance: Thales says water, Heraclitus fire, Democritus and Epicurus atoms; Pythagoreans add air and earth, making four elements.

2.2.2.g: All things arise from combining these elements in infinite kinds, so Vitruvius will treat materials' qualities so builders choose suitable ones.

2.3.1.g: Bricks should not be of sandy, pebbly or fine-gravel clay, which is heavy and washes apart; use white chalky, red, or coarse gravelly clay.

2.3.2.g: Make bricks in spring or autumn and dry them two years; undried bricks shrink away from stucco. Utica requires five-year-old bricks approved by a magistrate.

2.3.3.g: Three bricks: Lydian, 1.5 ft by 1 ft, used by Romans; Greek pentadoron five palms square for public and tetradoron four palms for private buildings.

2.3.4.g: Half-bricks alternate with whole bricks in courses to break joints on both faces; pumice-like bricks of Maxilua, Callet and Pitane float in water.

2.4.1.g: Pitsand is black, gray, red or carbuncular; the best crackles when rubbed in the hand and leaves no dirt on a white garment.

2.4.2.g: Lacking sandpits, sift river, gravel or beach sand; it dries slowly, forces pauses, cannot carry vaults, and sea-sand gives salty efflorescence under stucco.

2.4.3.g: Fresh pitsand dries fast and carries vaults but turns earthy if left exposed and cracks stucco; river sand suits stucco, not signinum.

2.5.1.g: Burn lime from white stone; mortar is 3 sand to 1 lime with pitsand, 2 to 1 with river or sea-sand plus one-third pounded brick.

2.5.2.g: Lime binds because kiln fire burns out stone's moisture and air, opening its pores; slaked in water it heats, then cools. Unburnt limestone never sets.

2.5.3.g: Limestone leaves the kiln the same bulk but about a third lighter; its opened pores let it mix with sand and unite with rubble.

2.6.1.g: Powder from Baiae and around Vesuvius, mixed with lime and rubble, sets hard under water; underground fires make the soil light and tufa dry.

2.6.2.g: Proof of subterranean heat: natural sweating-baths excavated near Baiae, and Vesuvius once vomited fire; sponge-stone or Pompeian pumice is burnt stone.

2.6.3.g: Sponge-stone occurs only near Aetna, the Mysian Burnt District and like places; fire has extracted moisture from tufa and earth as from limestone in kilns.

2.6.4.g: Fire-reduced unlike materials, suddenly saturated with water, effervesce with latent heat and unite into one solid mass; why Tuscany lacks such powder is posed.

2.6.5.g: Soils differ by country: sandpits abound on the Tuscan side of the Apennines, none toward the Adriatic or overseas; hot springs alone do not suffice.

2.6.6.g: Fire burning earth in Campania makes ash, burning soft stone in Tuscany makes carbuncular sand; one suits land buildings, the other piers under salt water.

2.7.1.g: Quarry stone is soft at Grotta Rossa, Palla, Fidenae, Alban hills; medium at Tivoli, Amiternum, Soracte; hard lava; white tufa of Umbria saws like wood.

2.7.2.g: Soft stones work easily but crumble in frost, salt and heat; travertine bears load and weather but cracks in fire, being mostly air and fire.

2.7.3.g: Anician quarries near Tarquinii, Lake Bolsena and Statonia yield peperino-coloured stone that resists frost and fire, being mostly earthy with little air and fire.

2.7.4.g: Old monuments at Ferento, statues and carved acanthus in Anician stone, look fresh; bronze-founders make casting moulds from it; if only it were near Rome.

2.7.5.g: Quarry soft stone in summer two years before building and leave it exposed; damaged pieces go in foundations, sound ones above ground. Same for rubble.

2.8.1.g: Two wall styles: opus reticulatum, handsome but prone to crack, and ancient opus incertum, whose imbricated rubble is uglier but stronger.

2.8.2.g: Build both with the smallest stones and abundant lime-sand mortar, because soft porous rubble sucks moisture from mortar and the wall falls apart.

2.8.3.g: Monuments near Rome faced in marble or dimension stone with rubble-packed cores are collapsing as porous rubble has drained the mortar's strength.

2.8.4.g: Leave a cavity behind facings; build inner walls two feet thick of red stone, burnt brick or lava, clamped to the fronts with iron, lead.

2.8.5.g: Greeks avoid soft rubble; they lay courses of lava or hard stone with alternating joints like brickwork, in two kinds: isodomum and pseudisodomum.

2.8.6.g: Isodomum has courses of equal height, pseudisodomum unequal; both are strong since dense stone keeps mortar moist and level beds bond through the wall.

2.8.7.g: Emplekton: finished facings with bonding stones; Romans carelessly fill the core with broken stone, Greeks build solid thickness with through-stones.

2.8.8.g: Rubble walls cannot last: arbitrators valuing party walls deduct one eightieth of cost per year, implying a life of eighty years at most.

2.8.9.g: Plumb brick walls are valued at full cost; examples: Athens' wall, Patras temple cellae, Arezzo wall, Attalid house at Tralles, Spartan paintings cut from brick.

2.8.10.g: More brick buildings: Croesus' house at Sardis, now a Gerousia; Mausolus' palace at Halicarnassus, brick walls with glass-like stucco and Proconnesian marble.

2.8.11.g: Halicarnassus is theatre-shaped: forum by the harbour, a broad street halfway up with the Mausoleum, fane of Mars on top, Venus and Mercury by Salmacis.

2.8.12.g: Salmacis spring does not cause lewdness: a colonist's shop by its good water drew Carian and Lelegan barbarians, who were softened by Greek customs.

2.8.13.g: On the far left stands Mausolus' palace, overlooking forum, harbour and walls, with a concealed harbour beneath from which the king could command secretly.

2.8.14.g: Artemisia hid her fleet in the secret harbour, lured the Rhodians inside the walls, cut a canal, towed off their empty ships; they were slain.

2.8.15.g: Artemisia took Rhodes in captured ships and set up two bronze statues, herself branding Rhodes; Rhodians later walled the trophy in and called it abaton.

2.8.16.g: Since rich kings chose brick, brick walls should not be rejected if properly topped; but reasons against them inside Rome will follow.

2.8.17.g: Law limits walls on public property to 1.5 ft thick; such brick walls carry one story, so crowded Rome builds tall with stone piers.

2.8.18.g: Outside the city, top crude brick walls with burnt brick about 1.5 ft high under the tiles, projecting as a coping to throw off rain.

2.8.19.g: Burnt brick can only be tested by exposure on a roof to frost and weather; hence the strongest burnt brick walls use old roofing tiles.

2.8.20.g: Wattle and daub burns like torches and cracks stucco; if unavoidable, set it on a high foundation clear of the floor. Timber comes next.

2.9.1.g: Fell timber between early autumn and the rise of Favonius; in spring trees are pregnant and loose-textured, as pregnant women are not warranted sound.

2.9.2.g: In autumn, fruit ripened and leaves withering, trees draw sap through the roots and regain solidity; winter air compresses them, so that is felling season.

2.9.3.g: Cut into the trunk to the heart and leave the tree standing until the sap drains out through the sapwood; only then fell it.

2.9.4.g: Fruit trees tapped at the base and pruned drain corrupting fluid and endure; undrained juices clot and rot, so drained timber lasts long.

2.9.5.g: Oak, elm, poplar, cypress, fir and other building trees differ in quality because of the different properties of their elements.

2.9.6.g: Fir has much air and fire, little moisture and earth: light, stiff, stays straight under load in framework, but decays and kindles quickly.

2.9.7.g: Fir's lower trunk is knot-free and, quartered for joinery, called clearstock; the upper part, cut about twenty feet up, is knotwood.

2.9.8.g: Oak, mostly earthy with little moisture, air and fire, lasts indefinitely buried underground, but exposed to moisture it warps and cracks structures.

2.9.9.g: Winter oak rots in damp; Turkey oak and beech soon decay; poplars, willow, linden, agnus castus are light, stiff, white, good for carving.

2.9.10.g: Alder, airy and fiery with little moisture, makes imperishable close-driven piles under foundations in swamps, though it will not last above ground.

2.9.11.g: All Ravenna stands on alder piles. Elm and ash, full of moisture, bend when fresh but seasoned become tough, good for dowels in joints.

2.9.12.g: Hornbeam is tough, used for yokes, hence Greek zygia; cypress and pine warp but their bitter sap keeps out decay and worms.

2.9.13.g: Cedar and juniper are equally durable; cedar-oil protects books from worms; Diana's statue and coffered ceilings at Ephesus are cedar; grows in Crete, Africa, Syria.

2.9.14.g: Larch, known along the Po and Adriatic, resists decay and will not catch fire, being dense moisture and earth; too heavy to float.

2.9.15.g: Caesar besieged Alpine stronghold Larignum, whose gate tower was of larch beams crossed like a pyre; soldiers piled brushwood and torches against it.

2.9.16.g: The tower survived the fire unharmed; townspeople surrendered and showed the trees, named larch from Larignum; larch eave boards would stop fires spreading in Rome.

2.9.17.g: Larch has pine-like leaves, long workable timber and honey-coloured resin good for consumptives; next: why highland fir is inferior to lowland fir.

2.10.1.g: The Apennines curve from the Tuscan sea; the shaded northern Adriatic slope grows large, moisture-swollen trees that dry hollow and frail, unfit for building.

2.10.2.g: Trees on sun-facing slopes are drained and solid-fibred, hence durable; lowland firs from sunny places are better than highland firs from shady ones.

2.10.3.g: Recap: materials, their elemental composition, merits and defects are done; the next book treats temples of the gods and their symmetrical proportions.

3.0.1.g: Socrates wished the human breast had windows; since knowledge is hidden, artists without wealth, fame, favour or eloquence cannot win belief in their skill.

3.0.2.g: Sculptors and painters who worked for great states and kings are famous; equally able ones serving humble citizens are forgotten through ill fortune.

3.0.3.g: Judges are swayed by social flattery and the uneducated are favoured; Vitruvius declines that contest and proves his knowledge by publishing this treatise.

3.0.4.g: Recap: book 1 covered the architect's training, healthy town sites, winds and streets; book 2 materials; book 3 will treat temples of the gods.

3.1.1.g: Temple design depends on symmetry, which arises from proportion (analogia): correspondence of the members' measures to the whole and to a standard part.

3.1.2.g: Human body proportions: face and hand 1/10 of height, head 1/8, foot 1/6, forearm and breast breadth 1/4; face divided into thirds.

3.1.3.g: A man lying with limbs extended fits a circle centred on the navel, and his arm span equals his height, giving a square.

3.1.4.g: Since nature proportions the body's members to the whole, the ancients rightly required exact symmetry in buildings, above all in temples, whose faults last forever.

3.1.5.g: Measures finger, palm, foot and cubit come from the body; the ancients and Plato held ten the perfect number, from the fingers and the units.

3.1.6.g: Mathematicians call six the perfect number, its parts being sixth, third, half, two thirds, five sixths; larger numbers are named ephektos, epitritos, hemiolios, epidimoiros, diplasios.

3.1.7.g: The foot is 1/6 of a man's height; the cubit has six palms or 24 fingers, so Greeks made the drachma six obols or 24 quarter-obols.

3.1.8.g: Romans first made the denarius ten asses, with the sesterce a quarter (2.5 asses); later combined six and ten into sixteen, the fingers of a foot.

3.1.9.g: As number came from the fingers and the body's members correspond to the whole, temple builders who harmonize parts and whole in proportion deserve respect.

3.2.1.g: Seven elementary temple forms: in antis, prostyle, amphiprostyle, peripteral, pseudodipteral, dipteral and hypaethral.

3.2.2.g: A temple in antis has antae projecting before the cella walls, two columns between them and a pediment above; example at the Three Fortunes.

3.2.3.g: The prostyle is like in antis but adds two corner columns opposite the antae and architraves returning right and left; example: Jove and Faunus, Tiber Island.

3.2.4.g: The amphiprostyle is a prostyle that repeats the same columns and pediment at the rear.

3.2.5.g: A peripteral temple has six columns front and rear, eleven per side, with a walk one intercolumniation wide round the cella; Roman examples by Hermodorus and Mucius.

3.2.6.g: The pseudodipteral has eight columns front and rear, fifteen per side, cella walls facing the four middle columns, leaving a walk two intercolumniations plus a diameter wide.

3.2.7.g: The dipteral is octastyle front and rear with two rows of columns all round, like Doric Quirinus and Chersiphron's Ionic Diana at Ephesus.

3.2.8.g: The hypaethral is decastyle, otherwise dipteral, with two interior tiers of columns, an unroofed centre and folding doors at each end; example at Athens.

3.3.1.g: Five classes of temple by column spacing: pycnostyle close, systyle a little wider, diastyle more open, araeostyle too far apart, eustyle just right.

3.3.2.g: Pycnostyle has intercolumniations of 1.5 column thicknesses (Divine Caesar, Venus); systyle of two thicknesses, plinths equal to the gap between plinths (Equestrian Fortune).

3.3.3.g: Pycnostyle and systyle are impractical: matrons must enter single file, doors and statues are hidden or shadowed, and walks round the temple are cramped.

3.3.4.g: Diastyle has intercolumniations three column thicknesses wide, as in the temple of Apollo and Diana; the wide spans risk breaking the architraves.

3.3.5.g: Araeostyle needs wooden architrave beams, not stone; such temples look low and broad, with Tuscan-style terra-cotta or gilt bronze pediment statues, e.g. Ceres, the Capitol.

3.3.6.g: Eustyle, the most approved: intercolumniations 2 1/4 column thicknesses, the middle ones front and rear three thicknesses, giving beauty, clear entrance and dignified walk.

3.3.7.g: Eustyle module: divide the front into 11.5 parts (tetrastyle), 18 (hexastyle) or 24.5 (octastyle); column 1 module thick, 9.5 high, gaps 2.25, middle 3.

3.3.8.g: No eustyle in Rome; the hexastyle of Bacchus at Teos is one. Hermogenes set these rules and invented the pseudodipteral by omitting 38 inner columns.

3.3.9.g: The pteroma was devised for the imposing relief of the colonnade and to shelter crowds from rain; the pseudodipteral achieves both, showing Hermogenes' ingenuity.

3.3.10.g: Column thickness to height: araeostyle 1/8, diastyle 1/8.5, systyle 1/9.5, pycnostyle 1/10, eustyle 1/9.5.

3.3.11.g: Shafts must thicken as spacing widens, since air seems to eat them away; corner columns are made 1/50 thicker to counter ocular deception.

3.3.12.g: Diminution at the necking by column height: up to 15 ft top is 5/6 of bottom; 15-20, 5.5/6.5; 20-30, 6/7; 30-40, 6.5/7.5; 40-50, 7/8.

3.3.13.g: Thickness adjustments compensate for the height the eye must climb; entasis, the swelling at mid-column, will be shown in a figure at the book's end.

3.4.1.g: Foundations go down to solid ground; stereobate walls under the columns are half again as thick as the columns, with intervals vaulted or filled with rammed earth.

3.4.2.g: On loose earth or marsh, clear the site and drive charred alder, olive or oak piles closely by machine, fill between with charcoal, then lay foundations and stylobates.

3.4.3.g: Columns are set on the stylobates by spacing class; in peripterals the sides get twice as many intercolumniations as the front, not twice the columns.

3.4.4.g: Front steps must be odd in number so the right foot arrives first; rise 9 to 10 inches, tread 1.5 to 2 feet.

3.4.5.g: A three-sided podium's plinths, bases, dies, coronae and cymatium must match the stylobate; the stylobate rises in the middle by scamilli impares to avoid looking hollow.

3.5.1.g: Column bases: height with plinth is half a column thickness, projection the same, so the base is 1.5 thicknesses in length and breadth.

3.5.2.g: Attic base: upper part 1/3 column thickness, rest plinth; upper part in four, one for the upper torus, the rest split equally between lower torus and scotia.

3.5.3.g: Ionic base: breadth 1 3/8 column thicknesses; upper third in seven parts, torus three, two trochili two each; astragals 1/8 of trochilus; projection 3/16.

3.5.4.g: Middle columns of front and rear stand plumb on their centres; corner and side columns have inner faces vertical and outer faces showing the diminution.

3.5.5.g: Ionic capital: abacus is shaft thickness plus 1/18, height with volutes half that; volute faces recede 1.5/18; height in 9.5 parts, abacus 1.5, volutes 8.

3.5.6.g: Volute setting-out: second line 1.5 parts inside; eye centre 4.5 parts below abacus, eye diameter one part; quadrants each shrink by half the eye diameter.

3.5.7.g: Capital: three of 9.5 parts hang below the astragal; echinus projects one eye; volute channel 1/12 deep; over 25 ft columns the abacus is diameter plus 1/9.

3.5.8.g: Architrave height by column height: 12-15 ft, half the bottom diameter; 15-20 ft, 1/13 of column; 20-25, 1/12.5; 25-30, 1/12; capitals follow stylobate curvature.

3.5.9.g: The eye weakens through thicker air at height, so upper members must grow; architrave soffit equals the column's top thickness, its upper face the shaft's foot.

3.5.10.g: Architrave cymatium is 1/7 its height; the rest in twelve parts gives fasciae of 3, 4 and 5; frieze 1/4 lower, or 1/4 higher if sculpted.

3.5.11.g: Dentils as high as the middle fascia, projecting equally; dentil face half its height, gap two thirds of face; cymatium 1/6; corona equals middle fascia; projection equals height.

3.5.12.g: Tympanum height is 1/9 of the corona front; raking coronae equal the lower; simae 1/8 higher than coronae; corner acroteria equal tympanum height, middle ones 1/8 higher.

3.5.13.g: All members above the capitals should lean forward by 1/12 of their height, because the longer sight line to the top makes them seem to lean back.

3.5.14.g: Each column has 24 flutes, hollowed so a turned carpenter's square touches both fillets and the curve; flute breadth equals the column's entasis.

3.5.15.g: Lion's heads on the side simae: one over each column axis, bored as water spouts, others solid over each tile row; closes the Ionic book.

4.0.1.g: Dedication to Caesar: recaps books 1-3 (architect's training, materials, Ionic temples) and announces book 4 on Doric and Corinthian orders.

4.1.1.g: Corinthian columns match Ionic except the capital: Ionic capital is 1/3 of column thickness, Corinthian the full thickness, so they look more slender.

4.1.2.g: Corinthian has no entablature of its own: it borrows either Doric mutules, guttae and triglyphs or the Ionic sculptured frieze with dentils and coronae.

4.1.3.g: The three orders are named from their columns; Doric arose first when Dorus built a fane in Juno's precinct at Argolis and others in Achaea.

4.1.4.g: Athens sent thirteen colonies to Asia Minor under Ion, who took Caria and founded Ephesus, Miletus and the rest; Melite was destroyed and Smyrna admitted.

4.1.5.g: The colonists expelled Carians and Lelegans, named the land Ionia after Ion, and built a temple to Panionion Apollo, calling its style Doric.

4.1.6.g: Lacking rules, the Ionians took a man's foot as one sixth of his height and made the Doric column six times its base thickness high.

4.1.7.g: For Diana's temple they made a womanly column 8 thicknesses high, with a base as shoe, volutes as curls, and flutes as robe folds.

4.1.8.g: Later taste fixed Doric height at seven diameters and Ionic at nine; the Corinthian order imitates the slenderness of a maiden.

4.1.9.g: A Corinthian maiden's nurse left a basket covered by a roof-tile on her tomb above an acanthus root; stalks grew up and curled into volutes.

4.1.10.g: Callimachus, called katatexitechnos by the Athenians, saw the basket, built columns on that pattern for the Corinthians and fixed the order's proportions.

4.1.11.g: Corinthian capital: height equals column base thickness; abacus diagonal twice that height; faces curve in 1/9; abacus 1/7 of capital height.

4.1.12.g: Below the abacus the capital divides in three: lowest leaf, second leaf, stalks with volutes; flowers equal abacus height. Other capitals form no new order.

4.2.1.g: Roof timberwork named: main beams on columns, tie-beams, rafters, crossbeams and struts for large spans, ridgepole, principal rafters, purlines, common rafters under tiles.

4.2.2.g: Stone temples copy carpentry: carpenters cut tie-beam ends flush with the wall and covered them with blue-waxed boards, giving triglyphs and metopes.

4.2.3.g: Mutules under the corona derive from projecting principal rafters, so in stone they are carved slanting downward as rafters do to shed water.

4.2.4.g: Triglyphs cannot be windows, since they stand at corners and over columns; metope means the space between two opae, the beam seats.

4.2.5.g: Dentils imitate common rafters as mutules imitate principal rafters, so Greeks never put dentils under mutules, nor either in pediments, only plain coronae.

4.2.6.g: The ancients approved only what can be explained by the truth of Nature, and so fixed each order's symmetry; the Doric is treated next.

4.3.1.g: Arcesius, Pytheos and Hermogenes rejected Doric for temples because of triglyph and metope problems; Hermogenes turned Doric marble into an Ionic temple of Bacchus.

4.3.2.g: Triglyphs should sit over column centres and metopes be square, but corner triglyphs make end metopes half a triglyph too wide, or end intercolumniations narrower.

4.3.3.g: Doric temple front is divided into 27 parts if tetrastyle, 42 if hexastyle; one part is the module (embates) governing all dimensions.

4.3.4.g: Doric in modules: column 2 thick, 14 high; capital 1 high, 2 1/6 wide in three parts; architrave 1; triglyphs 1.5 high, 1 wide.

4.3.5.g: Triglyph width divides into six parts: three femora, two channels cut to a carpenter's square, two semichannels; metopes square, half-module semimetopes at corners.

4.3.6.g: Triglyph capitals are 1/6 module; corona projects 2/3 module and is 1/2 module high with two Doric cymatia; guttae six broad, three deep.

4.3.7.g: The foregoing is diastyle; for systyle monotriglyphic Doric divide the front into 19.5 parts if tetrastyle, 29.5 if hexastyle, one part the module.

4.3.8.g: Each architrave span carries two metopes and two triglyphs, with half triglyphs at corners; the centre span takes three of each for a wider entrance.

4.3.9.g: Doric columns get twenty flutes; channel profile is the arc of a circle through the corners of a square whose side is the flute width.

4.3.10.g: Doric entasis follows the rule given for Ionic in book 3; the cella and pronaos arrangements come next.

4.4.1.g: Temple width is half its length; cella a quarter longer than wide; pronaos takes three parts; over 20 ft wide, two columns between antae with low screen walls.

4.4.2.g: Over 40 ft wide, add inner columns of equal height but thinner (1/10 against 1/8), with 28 or 32 flutes against 20 or 24.

4.4.3.g: More flutes make a column look thicker because the eye covers more points: a line round a fluted shaft is longer than round a plain one.

4.4.4.g: Cella walls are thick in proportion to size with antae as thick as columns; use small rubble or moderate uniform stones with bevelled joints.

4.5.1.g: Where the choice is free, the temple and cella statue face west, so worshippers at the altar face the sunrise and the statue.

4.5.2.g: If the site forbids, orient temples for the widest view of the city; riverside temples face the banks, as on the Nile; roadside ones face passers-by.

4.6.1.g: Doorways are Doric, Ionic or Attic. Doric aperture height is 2.5 of 3.5 parts of temple height; width 5.5/12; top narrowed by jamb fractions.

4.6.2.g: Doric jambs narrow 1/14 at top; lintel as high as jamb top; cymatium 1/6 of jamb, Lesbian carving; frieze equals lintel; plain corona projects its height.

4.6.3.g: Ionic doorway: width is 1 of 2.5 parts of the height; jambs 1/14 of height; cymatium 1/6; three fasciae of 3, 4 and 5 twelfths.

4.6.4.g: Ionic consoles hang to the lintel's bottom, 2/3 of the jamb wide and 1/4 slenderer below; door hinge-stiles are 1/12 of aperture, panels 3/12.

4.6.5.g: Door rails: height split 2 above, 3 below at the middle rail; rail 1/3 of panel width, cymatium 1/6 of rail, meeting-stiles 1/2, cover-joint 2/3.

4.6.6.g: Attic doorways follow Doric proportions with fasciae equal to 3/7 of the jamb; doors unlatticed, folding, opening outward. Tuscan style comes next.

4.7.1.g: Tuscan temple: width is five sixths of the length; the length is halved, the inner half for cellae, the front half for columns.

4.7.2.g: Tuscan width in ten parts: 3 each to side cellae or alae, 4 to the middle; columns 1/7 thick, 1/3 temple width high, diminished 1/4.

4.7.3.g: Tuscan base is half the column thickness, with circular plinth half the base and torus the rest; capital half a thickness, in three equal parts.

4.7.4.g: Tuscan main beams, coupled with dowels and dovetailed tenons, equal the column necking in thickness and keep a two-finger air gap to prevent rot.

4.7.5.g: Tuscan mutules project one quarter of the column height, faced with nailed casings; pediment in masonry or wood; eaves equal one third of the roof.

4.8.1.g: Monopteral round temples lack a cella: steps 1/3 of the diameter, columns as tall as the stylobate diameter, 1/10 thick, architrave half a thickness.

4.8.2.g: Peripteral round temple: two steps and stylobate; cella wall recessed about 1/5 of the stylobate breadth; cella diameter equals column height.

4.8.3.g: The rotunda's height, without the finial, is half the diameter of the whole work; the finial, without its pyramidal base, is the size of a capital.

4.8.4.g: Some temples keep usual proportions but move the front's features to the sides: Castor in the Circus Flaminius, Vejovis, Diana's grove, Athens, Sunium.

4.8.5.g: Some apply the Tuscan column arrangement to Corinthian and Ionic buildings, setting two columns in line with each cella wall where antae project.

4.8.6.g: Pseudoperipteral: walls moved out into the intercolumniations, dropping the pteroma to enlarge the cella. Plans vary because rites differ for each god.

4.8.7.g: Closes the account of temple principles, arrangements and plan differences, and announces the next topic: altars suited to the sacrifices.

4.9.1.g: Altars face east and stand lower than the temple statues; high for Jupiter and celestials, low for Vesta and Mother Earth. Book 5: public buildings.

5.0.1.g: Large books gain authority, but architecture cannot be amplified like history or poetry, which hold readers by novelty and metre.

5.0.2.g: Technical terms of architecture are obscure, so diffuse treatment hinders; Vitruvius will explain terms and symmetries briefly so they can be memorised.

5.0.3.g: He writes briefly for busy citizens; Pythagoreans composed books on the cube of 216 lines, with no more than three cubes per treatise.

5.0.4.g: A cube has equal square faces and rests firm on any side like dice; so cubic line-counts fix in memory; Greek comic poets divided plays by choral songs.

5.0.5.g: Hence short books, each class of subject complete in one; Books 3-4 gave temples, this book treats public places, beginning with the forum.

5.1.1.g: Greeks build square forums with spacious double colonnades, close-set columns, stone entablatures and upper walks; Italy cannot, because gladiatorial shows are held in the forum.

5.1.2.g: Italian forum: wide intercolumniations, bankers' offices in colonnades, revenue-earning balconies above; size by population; breadth two thirds of length, oblong.

5.1.3.g: Upper-tier columns should be one fourth smaller than lower, since lower bears the load and nature tapers trees such as fir, cypress and pine.

5.1.4.g: Basilicas adjoin the forum in the warmest quarter; breadth between one third and one half of length; surplus length takes Chalcidian porches, as in the Julia Aquiliana.

5.1.5.g: Basilica columns as high as the aisles are broad; aisle one third of the nave; upper columns smaller; screen one fourth lower than upper columns.

5.1.6.g: Vitruvius's basilica at Fano: nave 120 by 60 ft, aisle 20 ft, columns 50 ft high and 5 ft thick, pilasters 20 ft and 18 ft carrying aisle floors and roof.

5.1.7.g: Fano: windows between pilaster beams; columns four at each end, eight on forum side, six on the other, two omitted before the temple of Augustus and its hemicycle tribunal.

5.1.8.g: Fano hemicycle is 46 ft across and 15 ft deep; architraves are three two-foot timbers joined, returning from the third columns to the pronaos antae.

5.1.9.g: Over the capitals stand piers 3 ft high and 4 ft square, then a cornice of two two-foot timbers; tie-beams and struts carry one gable roof plus another over the pronaos.

5.1.10.g: The two gables meet like a letter T; omitting entablature, screens and second column tier saves labour and cost, while unbroken columns add dignity.

5.2.1.g: Treasury, prison and senate house adjoin the forum in proportion; square senate house height 1.5 times breadth; oblong, half the sum of length and breadth.

5.2.2.g: Senate house walls should be girdled halfway up with wooden or stucco coronae, which stop the voice rising and keep speech intelligible.

5.3.1.g: Theatre needs the healthiest site, as in Book 1: motionless spectators have open pores, into which winds from marshes bring noxious exhalations.

5.3.2.g: Theatre must not face south: sun heats air trapped in the curved enclosure, which burns and dries out the body's fluids.

5.3.3.g: Theatre foundations are easier on a hillside; on plain or marsh build substructures as for temples in Book 3; seats above of stone and marble.

5.3.4.g: Cross-aisle walls no higher than the passage is broad, else they throw back the voice; a line from lowest to highest seat must touch every seat edge.

5.3.5.g: Entrances should be many, spacious, straight, upper separate from lower, for unobstructed exits; the site must not be 'deaf' or echoing.

5.3.6.g: Voice is flowing breath of air felt by hearing, spreading in circular waves like those from a stone in water; obstructions throw waves back and break later ones.

5.3.7.g: Unlike water circles on a plane, voice spreads horizontally and also rises vertically by stages; unobstructed, all waves reach lowest and highest spectators without echo.

5.3.8.g: Ancient architects shaped ascending seats from study of the rising voice and used mathematicians' and musicians' canonical theory, like bronze or horn echeia on instruments.

5.4.1.g: Harmonics is obscure and needs Greek words lacking Latin equivalents; Vitruvius will explain it from Aristoxenus and append his scheme.

5.4.2.g: Voice moves two ways: continuous, as in speech (sol, lux, flos, vox), with no apparent pitch limits; and by intervals, as in singing, resting on definite pitches.

5.4.3.g: Three modes: enharmonic (two tones, two quarter-tone dieses), chromatic (two semitones, tone and a half), diatonic (two tones, semitone); each tetrachord totals two tones and a semitone.

5.4.4.g: Tone and semitone intervals of the tetrachord are fixed by nature in the voice; instrument makers follow these laws to perfect concords.

5.4.5.g: Each class has eighteen notes (phthongoi): eight fixed, from proslambanomenos to nete hyperbolaeon, and ten moveable, from parhypate hypaton to paranete hyperbolaeon.

5.4.6.g: Moveable notes shift by class: parhypate is a quarter tone from hypate in enharmonic, a semitone in chromatic; lichanos one, two, three semitones.

5.4.7.g: There are five tetrachords (text garbled: lowest ... conjunct synemmenon ... disjunct ... hyperbolaion) and six concords: fourth, fifth, octave, octave and fourth, octave and fifth, double octave.

5.4.8.g: Concords are named numerically: the voice passing from one note to the fourth note gives a 'fourth', to the fifth a 'fifth'.

5.4.9.g: No consonance exists across two, three, six or seven intervals in strings or voice; only the fourth, fifth and so on to the double octave are natural concords.

5.5.1.g: Make bronze vessels tuned to fourth, fifth up to double octave; set them inverted in niches between seats, free of walls, on wedges half a foot high, with openings 2 ft by half a foot.

5.5.2.g: Small theatre: one range halfway up with thirteen arched niches, twelve spaces; vessels from nete hyperbolaeon at the ends descending by fourths to hypate hypaton in the middle.

5.5.3.g: Voice from the stage strikes the vessels and wakes a unison note, gaining clearness; a large theatre has height in four parts with three niche ranges: enharmonic, chromatic, diatonic.

5.5.4.g: Middle range, from the ends: chromatic hyperbolaeon, diezeugmenon, synhemmenon, meson, hypaton, then paramese, descending by fourths.

5.5.5.g: No vessel in the middle of the chromatic range; top range: diatonic hyperbolaeon at ends down by fourths to proslambanomenos, with mese in the middle.

5.5.6.g: For ease consult the scheme at the end of the book, left by Aristoxenus, who classified the modes; following it perfects a theatre for the voice.

5.5.7.g: Rome's yearly wooden theatres need no vessels because boarding resonates, as lyre singers turning to the stage doors show; masonry theatres require echea.

5.5.8.g: Vessels are found not in Rome but in Italy and Greek states; Lucius Mummius brought Corinth's bronze vessels to Rome; poor towns use resonant clay jars.

5.6.1.g: Roman theatre plan: in the orchestra circle inscribe four equilateral triangles; the side nearest the scaena fixes its front, a parallel through the centre divides stage from orchestra.

5.6.2.g: Roman stage is deeper than Greek, since all perform on it and senators sit in the orchestra; height at most five feet; triangle angles direct stairs between cunei.

5.6.3.g: Seven angles give stairs; five fix the scene: royal door, guest-chamber doors, wing passages; seat steps a foot and a palm to a foot six fingers high, 2 to 2.5 ft deep.

5.6.4.g: The colonnade roof atop the seats should be level with the top of the scaena so the voice rises evenly; a lower roof checks it.

5.6.5.g: Cut away the lower end seats to a height of one sixth of the orchestra diameter to form entrances; set the passage soffits at that point.

5.6.6.g: Scaena length twice orchestra diameter; podium 1/12, columns 1/4 of diameter, entablature 1/5 of columns; upper parapets half, upper columns one fourth less.

5.6.7.g: Symmetry rules cannot fit every theatre: steps, cross-aisles, parapets, passages, stairways stay the same size at any scale; a skilled architect adjusts for site or scarce material.

5.6.8.g: Scaena has central royal double doors, guest-chamber doors either side, then periaktoi, revolving three-faced triangular scenery machines, and wings entering from forum and from abroad.

5.6.9.g: Three kinds of scene: tragic with columns, pediments, statues; comic with private dwellings, balconies, windows; satyric with trees, caverns, mountains.

5.7.1.g: Greek theatre plan: three squares inscribed in the circle; nearest side fixes the proscaenium, a tangent parallel the scaena front; arcs from two side centres complete it.

5.7.2.g: Greeks get a roomier orchestra, scaena further back and shallower stage, the logeion, 10 to 12 ft high; stairs follow square angles, increasing above each cross-aisle.

5.8.1.g: Choose a site where the voice falls gently; sites are dissonant (katechountes), circumsonant, resonant or consonant; dissonant ones throw the first sound back onto the next.

5.8.2.g: Circumsonant sites dissolve the voice in the middle, resonant ones echo and double case-endings, consonant ones support it; Greek theatres use squares, Roman equilateral triangles.

5.9.1.g: Colonnades behind the scaena shelter audiences from showers and house stage outfit: Pompey's, Eumenes' at Athens, Themistocles' Odeum roofed with Persian ship masts, Smyrna, Tralles.

5.9.2.g: Colonnades should be double, Doric outside; each aisle depth equals outer column height; middle columns one fifth higher, Ionic or Corinthian.

5.9.3.g: Colonnade Doric differs from temple Doric: height 15 parts, one is the module; thickness 2, intercolumniation 5.5, shaft 14, capital 1 high and 2 1/6 broad.

5.9.4.g: Ionic colonnade shaft divided into 8.5 parts, one the thickness; base half the thickness; Corinthian likewise with its own capital; stylobate uses scamilli impares.

5.9.5.g: The open space between colonnades should be planted: rarefied air from greenery clears gross humours from the eyes and draws excess humours from the walking body.

5.9.6.g: Proof: no mists rise from covered springs or underground marshes, only where the sun draws vapour in the open; so cities need roomy open-air walks.

5.9.7.g: To keep walks dry: excavate deep, build covered drains each side with earthen pipes inclined into them, fill with charcoal, strew sand and level.

5.9.8.g: Walks also serve as wood stores: in sieges salt, corn and water are easily got, but firewood for cooking is slow to gather and quickly consumed.

5.9.9.g: In sieges the walks are opened and wood allotted by tribes; they give health in peace and safety in war; baths follow next.

5.10.1.g: Baths face away from north; hot and tepid rooms lit from southwest; men's and women's hot rooms adjoin one furnace; three bronze cauldrons, hot, tepid, cold, feed one another.

5.10.2.g: Hanging floor: ground paved with 1.5 ft tiles sloping to the furnace; pillars of eight-inch bricks two feet high in hair-clay, spanned by two-foot tiles carrying the floor.

5.10.3.g: Bath vaults best of masonry; if framed, hang iron bars on hooks carrying unflanged tiles, clay with hair above, pounded tile and stucco below; double vaults protect timber.

5.10.4.g: Bath size by population; breadth one third of length excluding niches; washbowl under a window with roomy niche; basin at least 6 ft broad, step and cushion 2 ft.

5.10.5.g: Laconicum adjoins the tepid room, height to dome spring equal to width, circular; a bronze disc on chains at the dome aperture regulates temperature.

5.11.1.g: Greek palaestra, unusual in Italy: square or oblong peristyle with a two-stadia circuit (diaulos); three colonnades single, the south one double against driven rain.

5.11.2.g: Three colonnades have seated recesses for philosophers; the double one holds young men's hall, bag room, dust room, cold washing room, anointing room, cold bath, furnace, sweating bath, Laconicum.

5.11.3.g: Outside, three colonnades with running-tracks; the north one double, another single with edge paths at least 10 ft, sunk 1.5 ft to a track at least 12 ft wide.

5.11.4.g: The covered winter track is the xystos; beside it open walks (paradromides, Latin xysta) with plane groves and opus signinum resting places; a stadium behind.

5.12.1.g: Harbours with natural curving capes are best; build colonnades or shipyards round them and towers on both sides from which chains are drawn by machinery.

5.12.2.g: Without natural shelter, advance walls or embankments from one side; underwater walls use powder from Cumae to the promontory of Minerva mixed two to one.

5.12.3.g: Drive an oak-stake cofferdam with ties, level and dredge inside, fill with concrete; where the sea is too rough build a strong platform, part level, part sloping seaward.

5.12.4.g: Build marginal walls 1.5 ft thick, fill the slope with sand, cast a block on top, dry at least two months, cut the wall; waves undermine sand and the block falls in.

5.12.5.g: Without the powder: double-walled cofferdam of charred stakes packed with clay in rush baskets, pumped dry with water-screws, wheels and drums, dug to solid bottom, filled with rubble masonry.

5.12.6.g: On soft bottom drive charred alder or olive piles and fill with charcoal; build the wall of dimension stone with long bond stones and fill with broken stone.

5.12.7.g: Shipyards face north, since southern heat breeds rot and shipworms; never of wood, for fear of fire; sized for the largest ships; next book treats private houses.

6.0.1.g: Shipwrecked Aristippus sees geometric figures on the Rhodian shore, earns gifts by philosophy at the gymnasium; give children resources that survive shipwreck.

6.0.2.g: Learning is immune to fortune, revolution and war; Theophrastus: the learned man is a citizen of every country, the lucky man treads slippery paths.

6.0.3.g: Epicurus and Greek comic poets agree the wise owe little to fortune; Alexis praises the Athenian law requiring parental support only from children educated in arts.

6.0.4.g: Vitruvius thanks his parents and teachers for a liberal education in an art; holds that superfluity is useless and wanting nothing is true riches.

6.0.5.g: Vitruvius tells Caesar he never sought money, prefers slender means with good repute, and was taught to accept commissions only when asked, not solicit them.

6.0.6.g: The ancients entrusted work to well-born, educated architects who taught only kinsmen; now the unskilled profess architecture, so householders rightly build for themselves.

6.0.7.g: Only architecture is practised at home by amateurs because professionals are false architects; hence this complete treatise. Book 5 covered public works, Book 6 private houses.

6.1.1.g: House design must follow country and climate: different styles suit Egypt, Spain, Pontus and Rome, because regions lie differently relative to the sun's course.

6.1.2.g: Northern houses should be fully roofed, sheltered, with warm exposure; southern houses more open with a northern or north-eastern exposure, art amending nature.

6.1.3.g: Sun's heat dries bodies near its path; northern damp air fills them with moisture, making northerners tall, fair, red-haired, grey-eyed, full-blooded, deep-voiced.

6.1.4.g: Southerners under the sun are short, swarthy, curly-haired, black-eyed, short of blood: fearful of the sword but enduring fever; northerners are the reverse.

6.1.5.g: Voice pitch varies by nation: lines from north horizon to south and up to the pole star form a heavenly triangle shaped like the sambuca.

6.1.6.g: Southern nations under low heaven have shrill voices like the shortest sambuca string; pitch deepens through mid-Greece to the far north; universe composed in harmony.

6.1.7.g: Mid-latitude nations speak at middle pitch; northern voices sink to hypates and proslambanomenos, southern voices rise to paranetes and netes of the scale.

6.1.8.g: Experiment: two identical baked cups of equal weight and note; dip one in water and it sounds lower and weighs more, as moisture deepens voices.

6.1.9.g: Thin hot air makes southerners quick-witted; dense chill moist air makes northerners sluggish, as snakes are active in heat and torpid in winter.

6.1.10.g: Southerners are clever but lack valour; northerners brave but slow-witted and rash; the perfectly tempered middle territory is held by the Roman people.

6.1.11.g: Italy, like temperate Jupiter between hot Mars and cold Saturn, combines northern strength and southern wit; divine intelligence placed Rome to command the world.

6.1.12.g: Since nations differ by climate, houses must suit them; recap of the climate chapter, and next come the symmetrical proportions of house types and parts.

6.2.1.g: The architect first fixes exact proportions from a chosen standard part, then modifies by diminutions or additions for site, use or beauty without spoiling the effect.

6.2.2.g: Buildings look different close, high, enclosed or open; the eye deceives, as flat painted scenery seems to project and straight oars look broken under water.

6.2.3.g: Whether sight works by impact of images or by rays poured from the eye, as physicists hold, vision plainly can give false impressions.

6.2.4.g: Because appearance can falsify reality, proportions should be diminished or added to suit the site without loss; genius as well as science achieves this.

6.2.5.g: Settle the standard of symmetry first, lay out length and breadth ground lines, then build with eurythmy; the cavaedium is treated first.

6.3.1.g: Five cavaedium styles: Tuscan, Corinthian, tetrastyle, displuviate, testudinate. Tuscan has girders, crossbeams and valleys draining to the compluvium; Corinthian columns all round; tetrastyle four corner columns.

6.3.2.g: Displuviate cavaedium has outward-sloping beams shedding rain, suits winter houses but its pipes overflow and rot walls; testudinate suits small spans with rooms above.

6.3.3.g: Three atrium classes by length to width: 5:3; 3:2; or length equal to the diagonal of a square on the width.

6.3.4.g: Atrium height to girders is width less one fourth. Alae width: 1/3 of atrium length at 30-40 ft, 1/3.5 at 40-50, 1/4 at 50-60, 1/4.5 at 60-80, 1/5 at 80-100; alae height equals width.

6.3.5.g: Tablinum width is 2/3 of atrium width at 20 ft, 1/2 at 30-40 ft, 2/5 at 40-60 ft; small and large atriums cannot share proportions.

6.3.6.g: Tablinum lintel height is width plus 1/8, ceiling 1/3 width higher; fauces 2/3 or 1/2 tablinum width; ancestor busts at alae-width height; compluvium 1/4 to 1/3 atrium width.

6.3.7.g: Peristyles lie athwart, one third longer than deep; columns as high as colonnades are wide; intercolumniations 3 to 4 column thicknesses; Doric ones follow Book 4 modules.

6.3.8.g: Dining rooms twice as long as wide; oblong room height is half the sum of length and width; exedrae and square oeci 1.5 times width high.

6.3.9.g: Corinthian oecus: one tier of columns, architrave, corona, carved vault. Egyptian oecus: upper columns 1/4 smaller with windows between, walkway floor around, resembling a basilica.

6.3.10.g: Cyzicene oeci, not customary in Italy, face north onto gardens, have central folding doors and side windows, hold two sets of dining couches; height 1.5 times width.

6.3.11.g: Observe these symmetries where the site allows; where space is confined or walls darken windows, diminish or add with ingenuity so beauty resembles true symmetry.

6.4.1.g: Winter dining rooms and baths face south-west for evening light and warmth; bedrooms and libraries face east for morning light and to keep books from worms and damp.

6.4.2.g: Spring and autumn dining rooms face east; summer dining rooms north to stay cool; picture galleries, embroiderers' rooms and painters' studios north for steady light.

6.5.1.g: Private rooms (bedrooms, dining rooms, baths) need invitation; common rooms (entrance courts, cavaedia, peristyles) are open to all; ordinary men need no grand atriums.

6.5.2.g: Produce dealers need stalls, shops, crypts, granaries; financiers showy secure rooms; advocates roomy ones; magistrates regal entrance courts, large atriums, peristyles, libraries, galleries, basilicas.

6.5.3.g: Houses planned by class satisfy Propriety; same rules in the country, except town houses put atriums at the door and country seats put peristyles first. Farmhouses next.

6.6.1.g: Site farmhouses for health; size them by farm and produce, courtyards by cattle and ox yokes; kitchen on the warmest side, ox stalls adjoining with cribs facing fire and east.

6.6.2.g: Ox stalls 10 to 15 feet wide, at least 7 feet long per yoke; bathrooms and pressing room adjoin the kitchen; wine room next, lit from the north.

6.6.3.g: Oil room lit from the south; jars of about 120 gallons need 4 feet diameter each; lever-and-beam pressing room at least 40 by 16 feet, 24 wide for two presses.

6.6.4.g: Sheep and goat folds allow 4.5 to 6 feet per animal; granaries raised, facing north or north-east against weevils; stable in the warmest place away from kitchen fire.

6.6.5.g: Open-air cribs facing east sleeken oxen on winter mornings; barns for grain, hay, spelt and bakeries stand apart against fire; refined farmhouses may follow town-house symmetry.

6.6.6.g: Light test for town buildings: stretch a line from top of the obstructing wall to the intended light point; if ample open sky shows above it, light is unobstructed.

6.6.7.g: If timbers, lintels or upper stories block light, open higher up; put windows wherever sky is visible, including passages, ramps and stairs. Greek houses next.

6.7.1.g: Greek houses have no atrium: a narrow passage (thyroreion) between two doors, stables and porter's rooms beside it, leads to a three-sided peristyle with southern prostas or pastas recess.

6.7.2.g: Inside are large rooms where mistresses sit with wool-spinners; thalamos and amphithalamos flank the prostas; daily dining rooms and slave rooms surround; this is the gynaeconitis.

6.7.3.g: Grander men's quarters have four-colonnade peristyles; one higher south colonnade makes a Rhodian peristyle; Cyzicene dining rooms north, libraries east, exedrae west, large square rooms south.

6.7.4.g: Men dine without women in these rooms, the men's apartments; separate guest suites with own doors flank them; food gifts sent to guests gave paintings the name xenia.

6.7.5.g: Passages between the peristyles and guest suites are mesauloe, wrongly called andrones by Romans; likewise xystus, prothyrum and telamones differ in Greek and Latin use.

6.7.6.g: Male figures supporting mutules or coronae are telamones in Latin, atlantes in Greek, after Atlas who taught astronomy; his daughters are the Pleiades or Vergiliae.

6.7.7.g: The terminology was explained for scholars, not to change usage; Italian and Greek house plans are done; next, durability of buildings.

6.8.1.g: Ground-level houses last on proper foundations; with cellars and vaults, foundations must be thicker than upper walls, and walls, piers and columns set over their middle.

6.8.2.g: Insert wedged posts between lintels and sills at piers or antae, so loaded lintels and beams do not sag in the middle and ruin the walls.

6.8.3.g: Relieve wall loads with voussoir arches whose joints radiate to the centre, sprung over beam ends and lintels; wood then does not sag and is replaceable without shoring.

6.8.4.g: Where voussoir arches rest on piers, the outermost piers must be broader to resist the wedges' thrust pushing out the abutments.

6.8.5.g: All walls must be perfectly vertical; substructures need special care because earth filling swells with winter rain and bursts its retaining walls.

6.8.6.g: Make retaining walls thick in proportion to filling; build outer buttresses spaced at the substructure's height, projecting its thickness at the base and tapering to wall thickness.

6.8.7.g: Inside, saw-tooth walls project a distance equal to the substructure height, as thick as the wall; diagonal structures at corners distribute the earth's thrust.

6.8.8.g: Recap: buildings without defects have been shown; tiles, roof timbers and rafters need less care since they are easily replaced.

6.8.9.g: Materials depend on place and owner (brick, rubble, dimension stone); work is judged by workmanship, sumptuousness, design: credit to master workman, owner, architect respectively.

6.8.10.g: The architect should take advice from workmen and laymen; laymen judge only finished work, the architect foresees beauty, convenience, propriety. Book 7 treats polished finishes.

7.0.1.g: The ancients deserve unending thanks for recording their thoughts in treatises instead of passing on in envious silence, so learning could be refined over generations.

7.0.2.g: Without written commentaries we would not know the deeds at Troy, the physicists' views of nature, the philosophers' rules of life, or the kings' deeds.

7.0.3.g: Those who steal others' writings and publish them as their own deserve punishment, not just blame; the ancients chastised such plagiarists strictly.

7.0.4.g: Emulating the Attalid library at Pergamus, Ptolemy founded a library at Alexandria and set up literary contests with prizes in honour of the Muses and Apollo.

7.0.5.g: Ptolemy chose six citizens as contest judges and, on the librarians' advice, took Aristophanes, a diligent daily reader of all the books, as the seventh.

7.0.6.g: Six judges gave first prize to the poet the audience applauded most; Aristophanes voted for the poet who had pleased the audience least.

7.0.7.g: Aristophanes proved from named bookcases that all poets but one had recited stolen work; the king condemned the thieves and made him head of the library.

7.0.8.g: Zoilus Homeromastix came from Macedonia to Alexandria, read Ptolemy his attacks on the Iliad and Odyssey, then fell into poverty and begged the king's aid.

7.0.9.g: Ptolemy answered that Homer, a thousand years dead, fed thousands; Zoilus died as a parricide: crucified, stoned at Chios, or burned alive at Smyrna.

7.0.10.g: Vitruvius tells Caesar he neither retitles others' books nor wins praise by fault-finding, but thanks earlier authors and draws from them like water from springs.

7.0.11.g: Agatharcus painted a scene for Aeschylus at Athens and wrote on it; Democritus and Anaxagoras then wrote on perspective from a fixed centre and visual rays.

7.0.12.g: Lists Greek architects' treatises on their buildings: Silenus on Doric, Theodorus on Samos, Chersiphron and Metagenes on Ephesus, Pytheos, Ictinus, Philo, Hermogenes, Arcesius, and the Mausoleum.

7.0.13.g: The Mausoleum's facades were decorated by rival artists Leochares, Bryaxis, Scopas, Praxiteles, and perhaps Timotheus, making it one of the seven wonders.

7.0.14.g: Names lesser writers on symmetry and on machinery whom Vitruvius compiled; few Romans wrote on architecture: Fuficius first, Varro one book, Publius Septimius two.

7.0.15.g: Four architects laid foundations of Olympian Jove's temple at Athens under Peisistratus; about 400 years later the Roman Cossutius built its cella and dipteral columns for Antiochus.

7.0.16.g: Four places have supremely renowned marble temples: Diana at Ephesus (Chersiphron, Metagenes, Demetrius, Paeonius), Apollo at Miletus (Paeonius, Daphnis), and Ictinus' Doric cella at Eleusis.

7.0.17.g: Philo made the Eleusis temple prostyle; Cossutius built the Corinthian Olympion at Athens; Gaius Mucius built the Marian temple of Honour and Valour, not in marble.

7.0.18.g: Since Roman architects equalled the Greeks but few wrote, Vitruvius writes methodically; after houses in book six, book seven treats polished finishings, their beauty and durability.

7.1.1.g: For concrete floors, test and level solid ground or ram filling; under a timber-framed floor no wall should rise to the planking, or cracks form along it.

7.1.2.g: Use winter oak boards, not common oak, which warps; if forced, cut common oak thin, nail two boards at each joist end, then cover planking with fern or straw.

7.1.3.g: Lay fist-sized stone bedding, then broken stone with lime 3:1 (reused 5:2) beaten to at least 3/4 foot, then a 6-digit nucleus of pounded tile and lime 3:1.

7.1.4.g: Rub the laid floor down until lozenges, triangles, squares, hexagons or cubes lie in one plane; finish Tibur herring-bone brick likewise, then sift marble dust and coat with lime and sand.

7.1.5.g: Open-air floors suffer from damp, dryness and frost: lay a second plank floor at right angles, and mix new broken stone with one third pounded tile, lime 2:5.

7.1.6.g: Outdoors, beat the broken stone to at least a foot thick, lay the nucleus, pave with two-digit cubes sloping two digits per ten feet, and oil-dreg the joints yearly.

7.1.7.g: For greater care lay two-foot tiles in mortar over the broken stone, with finger-wide joint channels filled with lime and oil, then nucleus and cubes or herring-bone brick.

7.2.1.g: Lime for stucco must be slaked in lumps long before use; under-slaked lime hides crude bits that blister and break up the polished surface later.

7.2.2.g: Test slaked lime by chopping it with a hoe: bits sticking mean untempered, a clean dry iron means weak, glue-like clinging means ready; then build scaffolding and vaulting.

7.3.1.g: For vaulting, set cypress furring strips no more than two feet apart in a curve, nailed to ties of box, juniper, olive, oak or cypress, never common oak.

7.3.2.g: Tie flattened Greek reeds to the strips with Spanish broom cord, spread lime-sand mortar above; lacking them, use marsh-reed bundles knotted at most two feet apart, pegged on.

7.3.3.g: Render the vault underside, add sand mortar, polish with powdered marble; set slender impost mouldings beneath, without gypsum, and avoid the ancients' heavy overhanging soffits.

7.3.4.g: Mouldings should be flat in rooms with fire or many lights for easy wiping, and in relief in summer rooms and exedrae free of smoke and soot.

7.3.5.g: Apply a very rough rendering coat to walls, then when nearly dry sand mortar trued by rule, line, plummet and square, followed by a second and third coat.

7.3.6.g: After at least three sand-mortar coats, lay three coats of powdered marble, coarse, medium and fine, tempered so the trowel comes out clean; such walls will not crack.

7.3.7.g: Colours laid on wet polished stucco stay permanent because kiln-burnt lime, porous and dry, absorbs what touches it and sets with it into one solid mass.

7.3.8.g: Properly made stucco neither roughens nor loses colour when wiped; a single coat each of sand mortar and marble is thin, cracks easily and will not take polish.

7.3.9.g: Like a thick silver mirror versus a thin plate, thick compact stucco takes repeated polish and reflects the beholder clearly, while thin stucco cracks and fades.

7.3.10.g: Greek stucco-workers beat lime and sand in a trough with wooden beetles before use; slabs cut from old walls are reused as panels with bevelled edges.

7.3.11.g: On wattle and daub, prevent cracks by nailing reeds over the mud with fly-nails, daubing again, nailing a second row crosswise, then applying sand mortar and marble.

7.4.1.g: In damp ground-floor rooms render with burnt-brick mortar to about three feet; for a wholly damp wall build a thin inner wall with a vented channel and top airholes.

7.4.2.g: Without room for a second wall, make vented channels, lay two-foot tiles on eight-inch brick pillars a hand's breadth from the wall, and fix pitched hooked tiles above.

7.4.3.g: Whitewash the hooked tiles with lime and water so the burnt-brick rendering adheres, since kiln-dried tiles cannot hold it otherwise; then finish with burnt-brick mortar coats.

7.4.4.g: Wall decoration must suit the room: winter dining rooms, spoiled by smoke and soot, should have polished black panels with yellow ochre or vermilion blocks between.

7.4.5.g: Greek winter dining floor: dig two feet, ram, lay sloped rubble draining away, pack charcoal, then half a foot of gravel-lime-ash mortar whetted to a black absorbent pavement.

7.5.1.g: For spring, autumn and summer rooms, atriums and peristyles the ancients required pictures of real things; they began by imitating marble slabs, cornices and ochre blocks.

7.5.2.g: Later painters depicted buildings, columns and pediments, stage facades in exedrae, landscapes in long walks, and grand subjects such as gods, Troy battles and Ulysses' wanderings.

7.5.3.g: Current bad taste paints monstrosities: reeds for columns, fluted curly appendages for pediments, candelabra bearing shrines, stalks with seated or half-length human and animal-headed figures.

7.5.4.g: Such things cannot exist: a reed cannot bear a roof nor a stalk a figure; pictures unlike reality should not be approved even if technically fine.

7.5.5.g: At Tralles Apaturius of Alabanda painted a theatre scaena with rotundas and pediments above the roof; Licymnius denounced it as absurd, citing Alabanda's misplaced statues.

7.5.7.g: Apaturius altered the scaena to conform to reality; Vitruvius laments that costly showy colours now replace the painstaking artistic skill of the ancients.

7.5.8.g: The ancients used vermilion sparingly like a drug; now whole walls are covered, and costly malachite green, purple and Armenian blue are supplied by the employer by contract.

7.6.1.g: Marble for stucco varies: lumps with salt-like transparent grains are crushed, or workers' chips ground and sifted; between Magnesia and Ephesus it is dug ready-fine.

7.7.0.g: Colours are either natural products dug up in fixed places or artificial compounds of substances mixed in proper proportions.

7.7.1.g: Yellow ochre (Greek ôchra) is found in many places including Italy; the best Attic ochre, once followed as veins in Athenian silver mines, is no longer available.

7.7.2.g: Red earths abound but the best come from Sinope in Pontus, Egypt, the Balearic islands and Lemnos, whose revenues Rome granted to Athens.

7.7.3.g: Paraetonium white is named from where it is dug; Melian white from a mine on Melos in the Cyclades.

7.7.4.g: Green chalk is found in many places, best at Smyrna; Greeks call it theodoteion after Theodotus, on whose estate it was first found.

7.7.5.g: Orpiment (Greek arsenikon) is dug in Pontus; sandarach in many places, the best mined in Pontus near the river Hypanis.

7.8.1.g: Cinnabar was first found in the Cilbian country of Ephesus; its reddish iron-like clod sheds tears of quicksilver when struck during digging.

7.8.2.g: Clods dried in an oven give off fumes that settle as quicksilver; droplets are swept into water to unite; four pints weigh one hundred pounds.

7.8.3.g: A hundred-pound stone floats on quicksilver while a scruple of gold sinks, showing gravity depends on a substance's nature, not the amount of its weight.

7.8.4.g: Quicksilver is needed to gild silver and copper, and recovers gold from worn garments: burn the cloth, add ashes and quicksilver to water, squeeze through cloth.

7.9.1.g: To make vermilion, dry ore lumps are crushed in iron mortars, washed and heated repeatedly until impurities go; without its quicksilver cinnabar becomes soft and feeble.

7.9.2.g: Vermilion holds in closed rooms but blackens in sun and moonlight in peristyles and exedrae; Faberius' peristyle walls on the Aventine turned mottled after thirty days.

7.9.3.g: To preserve vermilion, brush melted Pontic wax with a little oil on the dry polished wall, sweat it with charcoal in an iron vessel, then rub with candle and linen.

7.9.4.g: This waxing is called ganôsis; cinnabar works moved from Ephesian mines to Rome after ore was found in Spain, and stand between the temples of Flora and Quirinus.

7.9.5.g: Cinnabar is adulterated with lime; test it on a red-hot iron plate: pure cinnabar blackens then regains its colour on cooling, adulterated stays black.

7.9.6.g: Malachite green comes from Macedonia, dug near copper mines; Armenian blue and India ink are named from the places where they are found.

7.10.1.g: Vitruvius turns to artificially made colours, beginning with black, which is indispensable in many works.

7.10.2.g: Black is made by burning resin in a small furnace venting into a marble-lined Laconicum-like chamber; the soot is mixed with gum for ink or size for frescoes.

7.10.3.g: Lacking that, burn pitch-pine shavings and splinters to charcoal, quench, and pound in a mortar with size for a serviceable fresco black.

7.10.4.g: Wine lees dried, roasted in an oven and ground with size give a black finer than ordinary, approaching India ink the better the wine.

7.11.1.g: Blue, invented at Alexandria and made by Vestorius at Puzzuoli: sand and natron ground like meal, copper filings added, rolled into balls, dried and fired in jars.

7.11.2.g: Burnt ochre is made by heating a clod of good yellow ochre to a glow and quenching it in vinegar, giving a purple colour.

7.12.1.g: At Rhodes white lead is made by laying lead on shavings soaked with vinegar in lidded jars; copper plates treated the same give verdigris, called aeruca.

7.12.2.g: White lead heated in an oven turns into sandarach, discovered through an accidental fire, and better than natural mined sandarach.

7.13.1.g: Purple, the costliest and most delightful colour, comes from a marine shellfish and varies in shade from place to place according to the sun's course.

7.13.2.g: Purple is black in Pontus and Gaul near the north, bluish toward the west, violet due east and west, and red in southern lands like Rhodes.

7.13.3.g: Shellfish are broken with iron tools, the purple fluid brayed in mortars; called ostrum from the shells, it dries up from saltness unless kept in honey.

7.14.1.g: Purple is also made by dyeing chalk with madder and hysginum; Attic ochre is imitated by boiling dried violets, straining through linen and braying with chalk.

7.14.2.g: Bilberry with milk gives fine purple; blue dyed with dyer's weed gives dyer's malachite green; Selinusian or anularian chalk dyed with woad (isatis) imitates indigo.

7.14.3.g: Book seven covered durable polished finishings, appropriate pictures and colours; with seven books on building done, the next treats finding, conducting and testing water.

8.0.1.g: Thales held water primordial, Heraclitus fire, the Magi water and fire, Euripides air and earth; Pythagoras, Empedocles, Epicharmus held four elements.

8.0.2.g: Nothing is born, nourished or preserved without the four elements: the body needs breath of air, right heat, and fruits of the earth.

8.0.3.g: Without moisture creatures wither; divine intelligence made the indispensable things (air, sun and fire, food, water) freely available, unlike pearls, gold, silver.

8.0.4.g: Egyptian priests prostrate before the waterpot, holding all depends on water; book eight will treat finding, qualities, conducting and testing water.

8.1.1.g: To find hidden water, lie flat before sunrise with chin on the ground, look across the country, and dig where vapours rise.

8.1.2.g: Water by soil: clay poor and shallow; fine gravel poor, deep, muddy; black earth slight but best; pebbles sweet; coarse gravel sure; red tufa copious; mountain foot abundant, cold.

8.1.3.g: Rushes, wild willows, alders, agnus castus, reeds, ivy indicate water, but not when growing in depressions that merely collect winter rain.

8.1.4.g: Test: dig a pit at least three feet square and five deep, place an oiled bronze or lead bowl inverted at sunset, cover; drops next day mean water.

8.1.5.g: Further tests in the covered pit: unbaked clay vessel goes soft, wool fleece can be wrung, a lamp stays unburnt and damp, a fire raises misty vapour.
