8.1.6.g: After the signs, sink a well, dig more nearby and join them by underground channels; northern mountain exposures give the sweetest, most abundant springs.

8.1.7.g: Mountain valleys hold rain and shaded snow that filters to springs at the foot; in plains the sun draws off the light part, leaving heavy, unwholesome water.

8.2.1.g: Rainwater is more wholesome, being drawn from the lightest parts of springs and filtered through air; rain falls mostly on mountains as morning vapour drives air.

8.2.2.g: Winds carry vapour from springs, rivers, marshes and sea up as clouds, which break against mountains and fall as water by their own weight.

8.2.3.g: Earth emits vapour and mist because it holds heat, air currents, cold and water; the rising sun on night-cooled ground raises mists, as in baths.

8.2.4.g: In hot bathrooms warm air lifts floor water to the vault until it drips on bathers; likewise the sun-heated air gathers moisture into clouds, like sweat.

8.2.5.g: North and northeast winds are dry and rarefied; south winds from the sun's course are damp, carrying moisture off and pouring it on northern regions.

8.2.6.g: Most great rivers rise in the north: Ganges, Indus, Tigris, Euphrates, Dnieper, Bug, Don, Phasis, Rhone, Rhine, Timavo, Po, Tiber; the Nile's course from Atlas is traced.

8.2.7.g: The Nile's source in Mauretania is inferred from springs west of the Atlas containing ichneumons and crocodiles, though no hippopotamuses.

8.2.8.g: Since large rivers flow from the north and Africa is dry, north or northeast springs are better, unless they meet sulphur, alum or asphalt.

8.2.9.g: Heat is not a property of water: cold water crossing a hot place boils up, soon cools again, but keeps the acquired taste, smell and colour.

8.3.1.g: Some hot springs taste excellent: fire in alum, asphalt or sulphur below heats the earth above, boiling sweet springs in upper strata without tainting them.

8.3.2.g: Cold foul springs like the Albula and Ardea rise deep, cross burning places and cool; compressed air makes them bubble and drives confined water up hills.

8.3.3.g: A covered bronze vase two-thirds full swells and lifts its lid when heated, settling when uncovered; so springs on hilltops sink when their channels are opened.

8.3.4.g: Hot springs heal: sulphur springs cure sinew pains, aluminous springs restore paralysed limbs by warmth, asphaltic springs taken as purges cure internal maladies.

8.3.5.g: Cold natron water at Penne and Cutiliae purges and reduces scrofulous tumours; springs near metal mines are copious but cause cramp and gout.

8.3.6.g: Water with a purple-glass scum at Athens is used only for bathing; at Troezen it causes foot disease; the Cydnus at Tarsus relieves gout.

8.3.7.g: The Himera in Sicily splits into a sweet branch and a salt one; lakes at Paraetonium, Ammon road and Casius are crusted with salt.

8.3.8.g: Oily and bituminous waters: Liparis at Soli, lakes in Ethiopia and India, Carthage spring, pitch at Zacynthus, Dyrrachium, Apollonia, Lake Asphaltitis, Jaffa, Arabia.

8.3.9.g: Water bursting through asphalt quarries carries asphalt out and rejects it; a Cappadocian lake between Mazaca and Tyana turns immersed reeds to stone overnight.

8.3.10.g: At Hierapolis boiling springs led into ditches between earth banks harden into stone within a year, making field walls; a rennet-like coagulating juice causes it.

8.3.11.g: The Hypanis in Pontus is sweet for forty miles, then 160 miles from its mouth a small brook from sandarach mines turns it bitter.

8.3.12.g: Soil gives waters their flavours as it does fruits: hence distinct wines such as protropum, catacecaumenites, Tmolian, Mamertine, Falernian, Caecuban.

8.3.13.g: Differing soil juices explain why aromatics, frankincense, pepper and myrrh grow only in Syria and Arabia, assafoetida in Cyrene; the sun's inclination causes this.

8.3.14.g: Rivers Cephisus, Melas, Crathis, Xanthus and some springs make white sheep that drink there at breeding bear whity-brown, gray or black lambs.

8.3.15.g: Deadly waters: the stopped-up spring of Neptune at Terracina, a lake at Chrobs in Thrace fatal even to bathers, a shunned fount in Thessaly.

8.3.16.g: By Euripides' tomb in Macedonia one stream is good, the other deadly; Styx water at Nonacris breaks all vessels but a mule's hoof and killed Alexander.

8.3.17.g: Deadly water in the kingdom of Cottius and a Faliscan grove spring; acid springs at Lyncestus, Velia and Teano break up bladder stones.

8.3.18.g: Acid soil juice sharpens these springs so they disperse bodily concretions; vinegar likewise dissolves an eggshell and turns sealed lead into white lead.

8.3.19.g: Vinegar turns copper to verdigris, dissolves a pearl, and splits heated lava rock; hence acid waters may cure patients with the stone.

8.3.20.g: A Paphlagonian spring intoxicates like wine; water of the Aequians in Italy and the Alpine Medulli causes swellings in the throat.

8.3.21.g: At Clitor in Arcadia a cave spring makes drinkers abstemious; a Greek epigram tells that Melampus there cleansed Proetus's daughters of madness.

8.3.22.g: On the island of Zea a spring makes drinkers lose their understanding; an epigram warns its pleasant draught leaves one dull as stone.

8.3.23.g: At Susa a little spring makes drinkers lose their teeth; its epigram says the water is excellent for bathing but knocks out teeth.

8.3.24.g: Springs at Tarsus in Magnesia give fine voices; near Juba's Zama, twenty miles off, Ismuc's soil kills serpents, even when carried elsewhere.

8.3.25.g: Caius Julius, Masinissa's son and Vitruvius's guest, told him springs there give fine voices, so people buy and mate handsome youths for progeny.

8.3.26.g: As the human body holds varied juices (blood, milk, sweat, urine, tears), the great earth holds countless juices that saturate water running through its veins.

8.3.27.g: Vitruvius's sources: his own observation and Theophrastus, Timaeus, Posidonius, Hegesias, Herodotus, Aristides, Metrodorus; aim is helping choose springs for aqueducts.

8.3.28.g: Nothing is so necessary as water: other foods can substitute for one another, but nothing lives without water, so springs must be chosen for health.

8.4.1.g: Test springs by the health of nearby dwellers; new water should leave no spot on Corinthian bronze and no sediment after boiling in a bronze cauldron.

8.4.2.g: Good water cooks green vegetables quickly, is limpid, grows no moss or reeds where it flows, and has a clean unpolluted bed.

8.5.1.g: Levelling uses dioptrae, water levels or the more accurate chorobates: a twenty-foot straightedge with equal legs, crosspieces with vertical lines, and plumblines.

8.5.2.g: In wind, use the chorobates' top groove, five feet long, one digit wide, a digit and a half deep; water touching the rims evenly shows level.

8.5.3.g: Against Archimedes' spherical water surface: the groove's two ends still stand level with each other; great fall eases conducting, depressions require substructures.

8.6.1.g: Three ways to conduct water: masonry conduits, lead pipes, clay pipes; channel gradient at least a quarter inch per hundred feet, arched over; city reservoir with three tanks.

8.6.2.g: Central tank feeds basins and fountains, the second baths for state income, the third private houses, so public supply never runs short and taxes maintain the aqueduct.

8.6.3.g: Through hills dig tunnels at the same gradient: cut the channel in tufa or stone, vault it in earth or sand, with shafts every 240 feet.

8.6.4.g: Lead pipes run reservoir to reservoir in lengths of at least ten feet; weights from 1200 pounds (hundreds) to 60 (fives), named by plate width in digits.

8.6.5.g: With lead pipes, carry water round small depressions; across wide valleys run down the slope onto a long low level substructure, the venter, before the rise.

8.6.6.g: Without a level venter, a mere elbow makes the water burst the pipe joints; water cushions must be built in the venter to relieve air pressure.

8.6.7.g: Build reservoirs every 24,000 feet to localise breaks, but only on unbroken level, never at a descent, on a venter, at risings or in valleys.

8.6.8.g: Cheaper: clay pipes at least two digits thick, tongued to fit, joints coated with quicklime and oil; bored red tufa blocks at the venter's elbows.

8.6.9.g: Air in an aqueduct bursts even stone, so admit water slowly and hold elbows with bands or sand ballast; add ashes at first filling to seal joints.

8.6.10.g: Clay pipes are repairable by anybody and give more wholesome water than lead, since white lead derived from lead is hurtful to the body.

8.6.11.g: Plumbers' deep pallor from lead fumes proves lead unwholesome, so water should not run in lead pipes; earthenware also gives purer taste than silver.

8.6.12.g: Without springs, dig wells, with care: earth holds the four elements, and air currents rising through fissures suffocate diggers who do not escape quickly.

8.6.13.g: Lower a lighted lamp into the well; if it goes out, dig air shafts right and left; on reaching water, wall the well without blocking the vein.

8.6.14.g: Where wells fail, collect roof water in signinum cisterns: sharp sand, lava bits under a pound, five parts sand to two lime, rammed with iron-shod beetles.

8.6.15.g: Clear earth between the beaten walls and ram the floor; cisterns in two or three compartments let mud settle; book nine will treat dialling.

9.0.1.g: Greek athletic victors get chariot triumphs and lifelong public revenues; authors, who strengthen all men's minds, deserve equal or greater honours.

9.0.2.g: Milo of Croton's invincibility benefited no one; the doctrines of Pythagoras, Democritus, Plato and Aristotle bear fruit for all nations and sound states.

9.0.3.g: Authors deserve palms, crowns, triumphs and consecration among the gods; Vitruvius will cite a few of their useful discoveries as proof.

9.0.4.g: Plato's problem: doubling a 10-foot square (100 sq ft) to 200 cannot be done by arithmetic, since 14 gives 196 and 15 gives 225.

9.0.5.g: Draw the diagonal of the 10-foot square, making two 50-foot triangles; a square on that diagonal holds four such triangles, doubling the area.

9.0.6.g: Pythagoras: three rules of 3, 4 and 5 feet joined tip to tip form a right angle; their squares have areas 9, 16 and 25.

9.0.7.g: The squares on sides 3 and 4 equal the square on 5; Pythagoras sacrificed to the Muses; the theorem serves for setting out staircases.

9.0.8.g: Divide the storey height into 3 parts; stringers are 5 such parts long, their feet fixed 4 parts out from the perpendicular.

9.0.9.g: Hiero of Syracuse vowed a golden crown, weighed out gold to a contractor, and received a finished crown of exactly matching weight.

9.0.10.g: Accused of silver substituted for gold, the crown was referred to Archimedes, who saw water overflow his bath and ran home naked shouting Eureka.

9.0.11.g: Archimedes made gold and silver masses weighing as the crown, sank the silver in a brim-full vessel and measured the overflow with a pint measure.

9.0.12.g: The gold mass displaced less water than silver, and the crown more than the gold mass, proving silver was mixed in and exposing the contractor's theft.

9.0.13.g: Archytas of Tarentum and Eratosthenes of Cyrene each solved the Delian problem set by Apollo's oracle: doubling the cubic content of his altar.

9.0.14.g: Archytas doubled the cube with semi-cylinders, Eratosthenes with the mesolabe; Democritus sealed tested principles with his ring in the Cheirokmeta.

9.0.15.g: The researches of learned men are an everlasting possession for character and utility, while athletes' fame declines with their bodily powers.

9.0.16.g: Though unhonoured, authors rise to the sky; lovers of literature carry the likeness of Ennius and the very figure of Accius in their hearts.

9.0.17.g: Posterity will converse as if face to face with Lucretius on nature, Cicero on rhetoric, Varro on Latin; absent authors outweigh living men.

9.0.18.g: Addressing Caesar: seven books treated buildings, the eighth water; this ninth gives the rules of dialling from gnomon shadows and why they lengthen and shorten.

9.1.1.g: The equinoctial gnomon shadow differs at Athens, Alexandria, Rome and Piacenza, so dials differ by place; the analemma is built from that shadow with compasses.

9.1.2.g: The universe is all nature and the starry heaven, which revolves round earth and sea on two pivots (poloi), one beyond the Great Bear, one under the south.

9.1.3.g: The north pole stands high, the south is hidden under the earth; an oblique broad belt of twelve equal signs inclines south and revolves with the heaven.

9.1.4.g: Six signs are always above the earth and six below, hidden by its shadow; as part of one sign sets, an equal part of the opposite rises.

9.1.5.g: The twelve signs turn east to west while moon, Mercury, Venus, sun, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn move west to east; the moon's circuit is 28 days plus an hour.

9.1.6.g: The sun crosses one sign a month and twelve in a year, the moon thirteen circuits meanwhile; Mercury and Venus wreathe round the sun, retrograding and pausing.

9.1.7.g: Venus follows the sun as Evening Star and precedes him as Morning Star; Mercury and Venus delay in some signs, then hasten to make up their course.

9.1.8.g: Mercury passes through all the signs in 360 days, averaging about 30 days in each sign.

9.1.9.g: Venus crosses a sign in 30 days when free of the sun's rays, pauses under 40 days in some, and completes her revolution in 485 days.

9.1.10.g: Mars returns in about 683 days; Jupiter takes 360 days a sign and 11 years 313 days; Saturn 29 months a sign and 29 years 160 days.

9.1.11.g: The three outer planets retrograde and pause while in the sun's triangle; Vitruvius rejects the view that distance from the sun darkens and hinders them.

9.1.12.g: Heat attracts everything, as crops rise and spring water vapourises; so the sun's triangular rays draw following planets and hold back those preceding.

9.1.13.g: The sun's rays run in straight lines as an equilateral triangle to the fifth sign, sparing nearer ones; Euripides' Phaethon says he burns the distant.

9.1.14.g: Jupiter's orbit lies between Mars and Saturn; planets nearer the earth with smaller orbits finish sooner and often pass under the higher ones.

9.1.15.g: Seven ants in seven concentric channels on a potter's wheel turned the opposite way: the innermost finishes first, like planets moving against the heaven.

9.1.16.g: Fire rises, so the sun heats Mars above him; Saturn near the frozen outer heaven is cold; Jupiter between is temperate. Next: the moon's phases.

9.2.1.g: Berosus the Chaldean: the moon is a ball half luminous, half blue; under the sun its bright side turns upward to him, making the invisible new moon.

9.2.2.g: Per Berosus the moon turns as it leaves the sun: thin line on day 2, half lit on day 7, full on day 14, then wanes.

9.2.3.g: Aristarchus of Samos: the moon has no light, mirrors the sun, has the shortest orbit; hidden at conjunction, thin edge on day 2, half lit on day 7.

9.2.4.g: The moon is full on day 14 opposite the sun, west at sunrise on day 17, mid-heaven on day 22, under the sun about day 28.

9.3.1.g: The sun marks the vernal equinox one eighth into Aries, lengthens days through Taurus and Gemini, and marks the summer solstice one eighth into Cancer.

9.3.2.g: Through Leo and Virgo the sun shortens the days, matching Gemini and Taurus, and marks the autumn equinox at one eighth of Libra, equal to Aries.

9.3.3.g: Through Scorpio and Sagittarius days shorten to the bruma at one eighth of Capricornus, then lengthen through Aquarius and Pisces when Favonius blows.

9.4.1.g: The Great Bear (arktos, helike) has her Warden behind; the Virgin bears the Harbinger of the Vintage and brighter Spica; Arcturus lies between the Warden's knees.

9.4.2.g: The Charioteer stands on the Bull's horn tip, sharing one star, with the Kids and She-Goat; Perseus above Bull and Ram holds the Gorgon's head.

9.4.3.g: Positions of the Fishes, Andromeda, Horse, Waterman, Cassiopea, Eagle, Dolphin, Arrow, Bird and Cepheus; one bright star joins the Horse's belly and Andromeda's head.

9.4.4.g: Above Archer, Scorpion and Balance the Serpent reaches the Crown; the Serpent-holder grips it and treads on the Scorpion; the Kneeler's head is near his.

9.4.5.g: The Kneeler's foot rests on the Serpent between the She-Bears (Septentriones); Lyre, Crown and Dolphin placed; Lesser Bear is kynosoura, Greater helike, tails opposed.

9.4.6.g: The Serpent winds between the Bears' tails with the star Polus; Cepheus' feet lie above the Lesser Bear's tail by an equilateral triangle of stars.

9.5.1.g: Southern Fish lies under the He-Goat, Censer under the Scorpion's sting, Centaur holding the Beast; the Snake carries the Bowl and Raven beneath Virgin, Lion, Crab.

9.5.2.g: The ship Argo lies near Bowl and Lion, bow invisible, stern joining the Dog's tail; Little Dog follows the Twins; Orion lies aslant under the Bull's hoof.

9.5.3.g: The Dog follows the Hare at Orion's feet; the Whale lies under Ram and Fishes, tied by the harpedonai; the River flows from Orion's left foot.

9.5.4.g: Constellations are given after Democritus, only those seen rising and setting; stars round the hidden southern pole never rise, as Canopus, reported from Egypt, proves.

9.6.1.g: Recap: the analemma is found from the firmament's revolution, the sun's contrary course through the signs, and the shadows of equinoctial gnomons.

9.6.2.g: Astrology and casting nativities belong to the Chaldeans: Berosus opened a school on Cos, then Antipater, then Archinapolus, who reckoned from conception.

9.6.3.g: Natural philosophers Thales, Anaxagoras, Pythagoras, Xenophanes, Democritus; then Eudoxus, Euctemon, Callippus, Meto, Philippus, Hipparchus, Aratus found star risings and weather signs through calendars.

9.7.1.g: Equinoctial shadow to gnomon ratio: Rome 8/9, Athens 3/4, Rhodes 5/7, Tarentum 9/11, Alexandria 3/5; it differs from place to place.

9.7.2.g: For Rome's 8/9 shadow: draw a ground line, erect the gnomon, divide it into nine parts, centre A at the ninth, radius to B: the meridian circle.

9.7.3.g: Mark eight of the nine parts on the ground line to C, the equinoctial shadow; line C through A is the equinoctial ray; diameter E-I is the horizon.

9.7.4.g: From F, where the equinoctial ray cuts the circle, mark a fifteenth of the circumference each way to G and H, giving the winter and summer rays.

9.7.5.g: Draw diameters G-L and H-K, bisect them at M and O; line P-Q through A is the axis; describe summer and winter semicircles on them.

9.7.6.g: Mark S and V on the horizon; the line G-H parallel to the axis is the Logotomus; a circle centred at D through H is the Menaeus, completing the analemma.

9.7.7.g: Hour lines are drawn on baseplates from the analemma for many dial types; all divide equinox and solstice days into twelve equal parts. Details omitted; inventors follow.

9.8.1.g: Dial types and inventors: Berosus' hollowed semicircle, Aristarchus' Scaphe and disc, Eudoxus' Arachne, Scopinas' Plinthium, Patrocles' Pelecinum, Dionysodorus' Cone, Apollonius' Quiver, plus portable hanging dials.

9.8.2.g: Ctesibius of Alexandria, a barber's son, first studied water clocks and discovered air pressure and pneumatics; he rigged a counterweighted mirror in his father's shop.

9.8.3.g: He fixed a wooden channel with pulleys under the roof-beam and ran the cord to a pipe where a falling leaden ball compressed air and sounded.

9.8.4.g: From that sound Ctesibius built the first water organs, water-raising devices, automata and water clocks, whose orifice is bored in gold or a gem against wear.

9.8.5.g: Steady inflow raises an inverted bowl, the cork or drum, driving a toothed rack and drum; further gearing moves figures, turns cones, drops pebbles, sounds trumpets.

9.8.6.g: A figure with a rod points to hours on a column; wedges adjust seasonal hour length; a solid cone fitting a hollow one regulates the water.

9.8.7.g: If wedges cause errors, mark hours transversely and month lines on the column from the analemma, and make the column revolve past the pointing rod.

9.8.8.g: The Anaphoric clock: bronze hour rods radiate over month circles; behind, a drum painted with the zodiac turns on an axis by bronze chain, cork and sand counterpoise.

9.8.9.g: As the cork rises the sand sinks and turns axis and drum; each sign has a hole per day, and a sun boss moved hole to hole marks hours.

9.8.10.g: Like the sun through the constellations, the boss moves against the drum's turn over wider or narrower spaces, showing hours and days of each month.

9.8.11.g: Behind the dial face place a piped reservoir with a bottom hole feeding a bronze drum, with a smaller drum turning inside it like a stopcock.

9.8.12.g: The larger fixed drum's lip has 365 points and the signs: Cancer top, Capricornus bottom, Libra right, Aries left; the smaller rim has a tongue and opening.

9.8.13.g: With the tongue in Capricornus the opening is perpendicular to the pressure, water enters fast and hours are short; in Aquarius the flow slows and days lengthen.

9.8.14.g: The opening climbs through Aquarius and Pisces to one eighth of Aries (equinoctial hours), to one eighth of Cancer (solstice, slowest), then down to one eighth of Libra.

9.8.15.g: The opening descends through Scorpio and Sagittarius to one eighth of Capricornus, restoring short winter hours; dialling is finished and machines follow in the next book.

10.0.1.g: Ephesian law: architect pledges property against his cost estimate; overrun up to one fourth paid by treasury, beyond that from his own estate.

10.0.2.g: Vitruvius wishes Rome had the same law for public and private building; a 50 per cent overrun ruins owners who budgeted 400,000.

10.0.3.g: Magistrates' shows of gladiators and plays allow no delay: seats, awnings and stage machinery must be ready on a fixed day, needing trained planning.

10.0.4.g: Since praetors and aediles must provide festival machinery yearly, the final book will teach the principles of machines, addressed to the Emperor.

10.1.1.g: A machine is a combination of timbers for moving great weights; three classes: climbing (akrobatikon), pneumatic (pneumatikon) and hoisting (baroulkos).

10.1.2.g: Hoisting machines raise and place weights and are the most useful; climbing machines show only daring; pneumatic ones give pretty effects.

10.1.3.g: Machines (mêchanê) need many workmen and great power, like ballistae and press beams; engines (organon) work at one man's touch, like the scorpio.

10.1.4.g: All machinery derives from nature: ancestors imitated the revolutions of sun, moon and five planets and improved their contrivances step by step.

10.1.5.g: Necessary inventions: the loom for clothing, yokes and ploughs for food, windlasses and press beams for oil and wine, carts and ships for transport.

10.1.6.g: Steelyards and balances prevent fraud; everyday machines such as mills, bellows, carriages and lathes are skipped in favour of rarer ones.

10.2.1.g: Hoist for temples: two timbers bolted at top, spread below, held by ropes; upper block (rechamus) with two sheaves, rope reeved to a lower block.

10.2.2.g: Socket-pieces on the legs carry a windlass turned by handspikes; iron shears on the lower block grip holes bored in the stone to raise it.

10.2.3.g: Three sheaves make a trispast, five (two below, three above) a pentaspast; heavier loads need thicker timbers with forestays and backstays tied to piles.

10.2.4.g: The large machine raises itself: a rope from its top block runs through a block on a pile and back to its own windlass.

10.2.5.g: For colossal loads the windlass is replaced by an axle-tree in sockets carrying a large central drum, which some call a wheel (text breaks off).

10.2.6.g: In drum machines the sheave rows are doubled top and bottom; the rope is middled at the lower block, both ends reeved up and down.

10.2.7.g: Rope ends tie to the axle-tree beside the drum; a second rope from drum to capstan turns it, or men tread inside a larger drum.

10.2.8.g: Single-timber hoist held by four stays, with cheeks, a wood piece two feet by six by four digits, and blocks of three sheave rows.

10.2.9.g: Ropes pass round all sheave rows to a third foot block (epagôn, artemon) with three sheaves; three rows of men pull without capstan.

10.2.10.g: This is the polyspast; the single timber can be inclined to set loads aside; the same machines load ships and haul them ashore.

10.2.11.g: Chersiphron moved column shafts for Diana's temple by leading iron gudgeons into their ends and rolling them in a four-inch timber frame drawn by oxen.

10.2.12.g: Metagenes enclosed architrave ends in wheels about twelve feet in diameter and rolled them likewise; feasible only because quarry is eight level miles away.

10.2.13.g: Paconius contracted to bring a new pedestal for the colossal Apollo, twelve feet long, eight wide, six high, with a machine of his own.

10.2.14.g: Paconius used fifteen-foot wheels with two-inch crossbars a foot apart and a coiled rope; the machine swerved sideways and he went bankrupt.

10.2.15.g: Shepherd Pixodorus found the Ephesian marble quarry when a ram's horn chipped white rock; he was renamed Evangelus and receives monthly sacrifice.

10.3.1.g: Hoisting machines work by two unlike elements together: the right line (eutheia) and the circle; neither alone can raise loads.

10.3.2.g: Axles are centres of sheaves and windlass; likewise an iron lever on a fulcrum (hupomochlion) lets one man heave a weight many cannot.

10.3.3.g: The lever's long head describes a circle and balances a great load; heaved upward, the ground acts as weight and the load's edge as fulcrum.

10.3.4.g: On a steelyard a small counterpoise moved far from the handle balances a very heavy object hung near it.

10.3.5.g: A pilot turns a laden merchantman with one hand on the steering oar (oiax); sails hoisted to the masthead drive faster than half-raised.

10.3.6.g: Like a lever pressed at its end, sails at the masthead push the ship harder with the same wind; oars on tholes work likewise.

10.3.7.g: Four or six porters carry loads on poles with straps at the centre marked by nails; a shifted strap loads the nearer man more.

10.3.8.g: Oxen pull equally with the yokestrap at the middle; shifting it makes one side longer to help the weaker ox; ends trace unequal circles.

10.3.9.g: Shorter arms bear harder as smaller wheels move harder; waggons, drums, mills, screws, scorpiones, ballistae and presses all work by axis and circle.

10.4.1.g: The tympanum raises much water but not high: a lathe-turned axle with iron-hooped ends carries a board drum divided by eight radial crosspieces.

10.4.2.g: Planks round the tympanum leave six-inch apertures; holes by the axle discharge into a trough; pitched and trodden by men, it irrigates gardens and saltworks.

10.4.3.g: To lift higher, a wheel as large as the height carries cubical boxes sealed with pitch and wax round its rim, emptying into a reservoir.

10.4.4.g: For still greater height a double iron chain over the wheel's axle carries bronze buckets of about six pints that tip into the reservoir.

10.5.1.g: River wheels have floatboards on their faces struck by the current, so the boxes raise water without any treading by workmen.

10.5.2.g: Water mill: a vertical toothed drum on the wheel axle drives a smaller horizontal toothed drum on the millstone; a hopper feeds corn.

10.6.1.g: Water screw: a round beam as many digits thick as feet long, ends divided into eight parts, with lengthwise lines and circles at one-eighth intervals.

10.6.2.g: A pitched willow or agnus castus withe is fixed obliquely from intersection to intersection; eight withes form spiral channels like a snail shell.

10.6.3.g: Withes build up until diameter is one eighth of the length, cased in pitched boards with iron bands; pivots in iron-sheathed holes; trodden by men.

10.6.4.g: The screw is set at the Pythagorean triangle's slope: length five parts, head height three, base four; a figure is at the book's end.

10.7.1.g: Ctesibius' bronze pump: two cylinders set apart, each with a pipe forking up to a middle vessel whose valves stop water returning.

10.7.2.g: An inverted-funnel cowl is wedged to the vessel through a staple, topped by a vertical pipe, the trumpet; valves sit in the cylinder bottoms.

10.7.3.g: Oiled, lathe-turned pistons worked by rods and levers force water through the pipes into the vessel and up the trumpet to feed a fountain.

10.7.4.g: Ctesibius devised many other water-and-air devices: singing blackbirds, angobatae, and figures that drink and move.

10.7.5.g: Only the useful was chosen: timepieces in the previous book, water raising here; amusements are left to Ctesibius' own commentaries.

10.8.1.g: Water organ: wooden base, bronze altar-shaped box, ladder-like uprights holding pump cylinders with wool-wrapped pistons; three-digit openings closed by cymbal valves hung from bronze dolphins.

10.8.2.g: Inside the altar an inverted-funnel regulator stands on three-digit cubes; its neck carries the windchest and kanôn mousikos with four, six or eight channels.

10.8.3.g: Each channel has a cock with iron handle opening ventholes from the windchest; oiled pierced sliders, called plinths, open and close the holes.

10.8.4.g: Iron jacks link sliders to keys; rings soldered over the board's openings hold the pipe reeds; valved pipes lead from cylinders to the regulator neck.

10.8.5.g: Raising the levers draws piston bottoms down and admits air past the cymbals; pushing up compresses it into regulator, windchest and channels.

10.8.6.g: Keys move the sliders to open and stop holes, producing melodies; Vitruvius admits the organ is hard to grasp without seeing it.

10.9.1.g: Hodometer for carriage or ship: wheels four feet in diameter cover twelve and a half feet per revolution.

10.9.2.g: A one-tooth drum on the wheel hub engages an upright drum of four hundred teeth in a case, which carries one projecting side tooth.

10.9.3.g: A horizontal toothed drum above has a hole per mile of a day's journey, each holding a stone that drops into a bronze vessel.

10.9.4.g: Four hundred wheel revolutions turn the upper drum once, equal to five thousand feet or one mile; each falling stone rings for a mile.

10.9.5.g: Ship version: an axle through the hull carries four-foot paddle wheels with floatboards; a one-tooth drum amidships engages a four-hundred-tooth drum.

10.9.6.g: A horizontal toothed drum in a second case holds round stones in holes; one drops through a pipe into a bronze vessel per step.

10.9.7.g: Under oars or wind the floatboards turn the wheels; every four hundred turns a stone falls, so sound and count give the voyage in miles.

10.10.1.g: Scorpiones and catapults are proportioned from the arrow's length; the hole in the capital for the twisted sinews is one ninth of that length.

10.10.2.g: Peritreti are one hole thick, one and three quarters broad; sideposts four holes high, five twelfths thick; middle post one and one eighth broad.

10.10.3.g: Arrow opening one fourth hole; pipe (syrigx) and cheeks nineteen holes long; bench one hole thick; windlass three quarters of a hole thick.

10.10.4.g: Latch seven twelfths long; trigger three holes; trough sixteen holes; standard twelve holes high on an eight-hole base with three nine-hole struts.

10.10.5.g: Antefix one and one eighth holes broad; rear support (antibasis) eight holes, prop twelve; cushion two and a half; arm seven holes long.

10.10.6.g: High-tensioned capitals take shorter arms, low-tensioned longer; a five-foot lever needs four men, a ten-foot lever two.

10.11.1.g: Ballistae are worked by windlasses, pulleys, capstans or drums, but all are computed from the weight of stone to be thrown, needing geometry.

10.11.2.g: Ballista holes, strung with twisted women's hair or sinew, follow the stone's weight; Vitruvius will give tested values converted from Greek to Roman weights.

10.11.3.g: Table of ballista holes: two-pound stone five digits, ten pounds eight, up to 360 pounds one foot ten digits.

10.11.4.g: The scutula (peritrêtos) is two and one sixth holes broad, a rhomboid reduced one sixth in length and one fourth in breadth, then curved.

10.11.5.g: Scutula seven twelfths of a hole thick; boxes two holes high, one and three quarters broad; sideposts five and two thirds long, thirty-seven forty-eighths thick.

10.11.6.g: Inner table strip eight holes long, half a hole broad and thick, tenons one and one sixth, curvature three quarters; crosspieces half a hole.

10.11.7.g: Ladder shafts thirteen holes long, one thick, one and a quarter apart; chelônion takes two fifths, eleven and a half long; claw projects half.

10.11.8.g: Inner slips one quarter hole broad, one sixth thick; chelonium lid three sixteenths by one twelfth; round axle seven sixteenths at the pivots.

10.11.9.g: Stays one quarter hole broad; supporter one and a half holes square; ballista arm six holes long, two thirds thick at base, half at end.

10.12.1.g: Stretching frame: long beams with socket-pieces for windlasses; capitals wedged into cuttings midway; bronze boxes and iron bolts (epizygides) inserted.

10.12.2.g: String loops are passed through the capital holes, stretched on windlasses until both sides sound the same note when struck, then wedged tight.

10.13.1.g: The battering ram arose when Carthaginians besieging Cadiz, lacking iron tools, drove a hand-held beam against a wall and demolished it course by course.

10.13.2.g: A Tyrian carpenter (Bright) hung the ram from a mast like a steelyard; Geras of Chalcedon put it in a wheeled, oxhide-covered frame, the tortoise.

10.13.3.g: Polyidus the Thessalian improved siege engines under Philip at Byzantium; his pupil Diades invented moveable towers, the borer, scaling machine and raven.

10.13.4.g: Diades' smallest tower: at least sixty cubits high, seventeen broad, one fifth less at top, uprights nine inches to half a foot, ten stories.

10.13.5.g: Diades' larger tower: 120 cubits high, twenty-three and a half broad, twenty stories with three-cubit galleries, uprights one foot to six digits, rawhide covered.

10.13.6.g: Ram tortoise: base thirty cubits square, thirteen high, pediment seven, with a four-story turret holding scorpiones and water; ram swings on a roller (kriodochê).

10.13.7.g: The borer resembles the tortoise with a pipe fifty cubits long and one high, with windlass, blocks, rollers and an iron-pointed beam under rawhide arches.

10.13.8.g: Diades dismissed the raven as worthless and never explained the scaling machine (epibathra) or naval boarding devices; Vitruvius turns to his teachers' methods.

10.14.1.g: Ditch-filling tortoise: base (eschara) twenty-one feet square with four crosspieces three and a half feet apart, on pivoted trees levered to move any way.

10.14.2.g: Beams project six and seven feet; posts nine feet high, one and a quarter square, one and a half apart; rafters rise twelve feet.

10.14.3.g: Rafters are bridged and boarded, preferably in holm oak, never pine or alder; then fresh wattles and double rawhide stuffed with vinegar-soaked seaweed or straw.

10.15.1.g: Another tortoise has parapet, battlements and sloping eaves with clay-and-hair coating and up to eight wheels; excavating tortoises (oryktides) have triangular fronts.

10.15.2.g: Hegetor's tortoise: base sixty-three by forty-two feet, four corner posts thirty-six feet high, eight wheels six and three quarters feet high, three thick.

10.15.3.g: Posts eighteen feet high, three quarters by two thirds foot, one and three quarters apart; beams a foot broad; rafters rise twelve feet, floored over.

10.15.4.g: A middle floor held scorpiones and catapults; two framed uprights forty-five feet long carried a block with two axles from which ropes held the ram.

10.15.5.g: A turret-like parapet above sheltered two lookouts; the ram was 180 feet long, a foot and a quarter by a foot, tapering at the head.

10.15.6.g: The ram had a warship-like iron beak, four fifteen-foot iron plates, three eight-digit cables girdled every foot and a quarter, rawhide wrap, fourfold chains.

10.15.7.g: A netted box at the ram's end gave footing; it moved six ways, reached one hundred feet, weighed 4000 talents, worked by 100 men.

10.16.1.g: Ladders and cranes are omitted as soldiers build them; machines must vary, since fortifications and the bravery of nations differ.

10.16.2.g: Combining these principles suffices to design any machine; defence needs no treatise, since quick shrewd plans often foil engines, as the Rhodians found.

10.16.3.g: Rhodian architect Diognetus lost his public salary to Callias of Aradus, who showed a model crane seizing a helepolis and lifting it inside the wall.

10.16.4.g: Epimachus built Demetrius Poliorcetes a helepolis 135 feet high, sixty broad, weighing 360,000 pounds, proof against 360-pound stones; Callias said he could not seize it.

10.16.5.g: Models do not always scale: an auger bores half-inch to inch-and-a-half holes, but a quarter-foot hole is impracticable and half a foot inconceivable.

10.16.6.g: Deceived by the model, the Rhodians had wronged Diognetus; facing slavery they fell at his feet begging help, and he at first refused.

10.16.7.g: Diognetus pierced the wall and poured water, filth and excrement through pipes overnight; the helepolis stuck in the swamp and Demetrius withdrew.

10.16.8.g: The Rhodians honoured Diognetus, who set the helepolis in a public place with a dedicatory inscription; defence needs wise plans above machines.

10.16.9.g: The Chians dumped earth, sand and stones offshore so enemy ships with storming bridges grounded and burned; Apollonia feared mines of unknown place.

10.16.10.g: Trypho of Alexandria dug countermines hung with bronze vessels that rang at enemy digging, then poured boiling water, pitch, excrement and hot sand on them.

10.16.11.g: At Marseilles over thirty mines were defeated by deepening the moat and by a huge basin within the walls that flooded and collapsed them.

10.16.12.g: Massiliots burned a rampart with red-hot ballista bolts and noosed a ram's head by capstan; architects' cunning saves states. The ten books conclude.
